issues.summary: Platform Foundation
issues.description:
The `aria` Cargo workspace, the shared `proto/` directory and its codegen, the CI skeleton, and the working conventions every other epic builds on. One monorepo, one crate per service; protobuf schemas versioned independently per service with `tonic`/`prost` codegen wired up.

**Not this epic:** container image build/publish and cluster deploy (ARIA-8); OpenTelemetry instrumentation (ARIA-9); the Self-Extension server's own repo and CI (ARIA-10). Each service epic owns its own `.proto` service definition — this epic owns the directory, the versioning convention and the codegen.

**Decisions**

* D14 — generated code is built into `OUT_DIR` and never committed, so there is no freshness check to build; CI narrows to build, test, lint plus protobuf lint and breaking-change detection
* D15 — one umbrella Helm chart for the whole `aria` namespace, settling the manifests-vs-chart convention this epic used to hold open

**Links:** [Decision Log — repo, proto & CI](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/decisions/0002-repo-proto-ci.md) · [Conventions](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/05-conventions.md)

issues.summary: Keycloak Integration & aria-identity
issues.description:
Register ARIA in the existing shared homelab Keycloak realm, and build `aria-identity` — the library crate every service uses to validate tokens, authenticate to peers, and sign or verify the propagated end-user context. Also owns the per-MCP-server confidential clients with `consent required` and their declared scopes.

**Not this epic:** minting the end-user context from a validated JWT (ARIA-4); the `consent_grants` / `mcp_tools` / `consent_audit_log` tables (ARIA-3); enforcing consent at call time (ARIA-7). There is no user-service to build — Keycloak's job is strictly authN/authZ, not preferences or relationships.

**Decisions**

* D7 — the scope-naming convention this epic used to hold open is settled: one scope per tool, `aria:mcp:<server-slug>:<tool>`

**Links:** [Decision Log — identity & tokens](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/decisions/0001-identity-tokens-service-auth.md) · [Identity](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/services/identity.md)

issues.summary: Knowledge Core
issues.description:
`aria-knowledge-core` — the RAG system at the centre of ARIA. Owns Postgres (the social graph, preferences, calendar, the MCP server registry and the consent tables) and Qdrant (embeddings of facts, preferences and conversation history), exposed over gRPC. Replaces `DB-ARIA`, `DB-ARIA-User`, `DB-Connect` and the hand-built sharded graph store.

**Not this epic:** deploying Postgres and Qdrant (ARIA-8 owns the operator, StatefulSets and volumes); retrieval invocation in the request path (ARIA-6); consent _enforcement_ (ARIA-7); Keycloak-side client and scope config (ARIA-2).

**Decisions**

* D16 + D48 — the typed/free-text split and its classification rule settle what is embedded into Qdrant versus kept as typed Postgres attributes
* D21 — MCP service writes are namespaced by source with areas declared at registration, settling what write access a connected service has

**Links:** [Decision Log — knowledge model](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/decisions/0003-knowledge-model.md) · [Knowledge Core](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/services/knowledge-core.md)

issues.summary: Gateway
issues.description:
`aria-gateway` — the client-facing gRPC endpoint for voice streaming and text/command input, and the single trust boundary where a raw user credential exists. Validates the Keycloak JWT at the edge and mints the minimal signed end-user context attached to every downstream call — injected by trusted infrastructure only, **never** an LLM-fillable tool argument. Replaces the three hand-wrapped SSL sockets of the 2021 design.

**Not this epic:** the validation and context-signing primitives themselves (ARIA-2); STT/TTS (ARIA-5); orchestration (ARIA-6). A minimal CLI test client for the streaming audio path is in scope as a harness; there is no commitment to the original iOS or Android client plans, and external/remote access is deferred project-wide.

**Links:** [Decision Log — identity & tokens](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/decisions/0001-identity-tokens-service-auth.md) · [Gateway](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/services/gateway.md)

issues.summary: Speech
issues.description:
`aria-speech` — STT and TTS only, as a gRPC service scheduled onto the GPU node already running Ollama, reusing whatever GPU runtime config already makes Ollama work there. Model selection and memory headroom against the co-resident Ollama model is a first-class concern of this epic, not an afterthought.

**Not this epic:** audio transport to and from clients (ARIA-4 owns the bidirectional streaming channel); the nodeSelector and GPU scheduling manifests (ARIA-8) — though the memory-budgeting analysis belongs here.

**Links:** [Decision Log — audio pipeline](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/decisions/0004-audio-pipeline.md) · [Speech](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/services/speech.md) · [ARIA-27 GPU baseline](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/spikes/ARIA-27-gpu-baseline.md)

issues.summary: Agent Core (DEC)
issues.description:
`aria-agent-core` — the orchestrator and MCP Host. Per request: retrieve context from the Knowledge Core, call the pluggable LLM with the current MCP toolset, execute whichever tool call the model chooses via the MCP Registry, return the response. Unrecognized requests are logged back to the Knowledge Core, replacing the old `Unknown` fallback and the hand-built NLU/NLG boxes. The hosted frontier API is the default backend; the existing Ollama instance is wired in behind the same interface from day one as the fallback.

**Not this epic:** MCP server connections, tool aggregation and consent enforcement (ARIA-7); the Knowledge Core's storage and schema (ARIA-3); STT/TTS (ARIA-5).

**Decisions**

* D35 — failover plus an explicit override; automatic cost/offline routing is deferred, not open

**Open**

* The specific hosted provider and model for the default backend (ARIA-40)

**Links:** [Decision Log — Agent Core & sessions](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/decisions/0006-agent-core-sessions.md) · [Agent Core](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/services/agent-core.md)

issues.summary: MCP Registry
issues.description:
`aria-mcp-registry` — the control plane that connects ARIA to new MCP servers at runtime, aggregates their tools, and enforces consent before any tool call is forwarded. Default transport is HTTP (streamable HTTP/SSE), **not** stdio, to fit the Kubernetes deployment; it also owns the shared `mcp-client` crate. Before forwarding it checks both gates — the user's Keycloak-level consent for that server, and an active per-tool grant — regardless of what the target server does internally, and writes every invocation to `consent_audit_log`. Standard, unmodified MCP: the protocol is never forked.

**Not this epic:** the consent tables themselves (ARIA-3); Keycloak per-server client config (ARIA-2); the LLM tool-calling loop (ARIA-6).

**Open**

* Which Rust MCP SDK to standardise on for this service (ARIA-65) — D38 settled that the Agent Core uses none, so the question is now the Registry's alone

**Links:** [Decision Log — observability & consent](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/decisions/0007-observability-consent.md) · [MCP Registry](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/services/mcp-registry.md)

issues.summary: Deployment & Infra
issues.description:
Deploy ARIA into its own `aria` namespace on the existing k3s cluster — reusing what already runs and adding only what is genuinely new. Keycloak and Ollama are reused with no new deployment; ARIA's services deploy as Deployments, Postgres and Qdrant as StatefulSets with persistent volumes, and Speech is pinned to the GPU node. Owns container image build/publish and cluster deploy.

**Not this epic:** build, test and lint CI (ARIA-1). Explicit non-goal: standing up new infrastructure that duplicates what already runs — Keycloak, Ollama, Kubernetes. External/remote access is deferred.

**Decisions**

* D15 — one umbrella Helm chart for the whole namespace, settling the manifests-vs-chart convention this epic co-owned with ARIA-1

**Open**

* Which Postgres operator and which Qdrant deployment topology to use in-cluster

**Links:** [Decision Log — secrets & deployment](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/decisions/0005-secrets-deployment.md) · [Deployment](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/04-deployment.md)

issues.summary: Observability
issues.description:
Instrument every ARIA service with OpenTelemetry — `tracing` + `tracing-opentelemetry` + `opentelemetry-otlp`, deliberately vendor-neutral — and export to AppSignal via its **self-hosted, in-cluster** collector rather than their hosted one. The collector is the one place to enforce that conversation and voice content never lands in a span attribute or log line; that scrubbing is a first-class deliverable, not a nice-to-have. AppSignal's Rust support is OpenTelemetry-based and currently beta, which vendor-neutral instrumentation exists to absorb.

**Not this epic:** the collector's Helm chart and workload manifests (ARIA-8) — this epic owns its configuration and pipeline.

**Open**

* AppSignal's billable-request definition, confirmed against ARIA's per-interaction fan-out across 5+ internal services rather than assumed against the free tier

**Links:** [Decision Log — observability & consent](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/decisions/0007-observability-consent.md) · [Deployment](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/04-deployment.md)

issues.summary: Self-Extension MCP Server
issues.description:
The first MCP server ARIA gets: the one that lets her design, generate, test and — only after Jann approves — deploy new MCP servers herself. Proposed tools: `draft_service`, `generate_code`, `run_tests`, `request_approval`, `deploy_service`. It lives in a **separate repo outside the** `aria` monorepo, like any other MCP server, and owns its own approval CI. Name TBD.

**Not this epic:** consent enforcement on this server's tools, which the MCP Registry applies like any other server (ARIA-7) — defense in depth, which matters most for self-generated servers.

**Decisions**

* D34 — the approval pipeline seals a new service's credentials, settling the credential-provisioning question this epic used to hold open

**Open**

* Whether a GitHub PR is the right approval surface for `request_approval`, or whether some approvals should be conversational — the two can coexist for different stakes
* Where sandboxed `run_tests` execution runs for a candidate service — a disposable namespace or pod on the existing cluster is the natural default
* How a server's declared tools get a risk tier, if any, during `draft_service` or registration

**Links:** [Decision Log — observability & consent](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/decisions/0007-observability-consent.md) · [Decision Log — secrets & deployment](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/decisions/0005-secrets-deployment.md) · [Self-Extension](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/services/self-extension.md)

issues.description:
Stand up the empty monorepo structure that every other crate lands in.

**From CLAUDE.md §5:** "Single `aria` monorepo (Cargo workspace) for now — the names below double as container image tags today and as standalone repo names if any service is ever split out later." Paths: `services/gateway/`, `services/speech/`, `services/agent-core/`, `services/mcp-registry/`, `services/knowledge-core/`, `crates/identity/`, `proto/`.

**Acceptance criteria:**

* A root `Cargo.toml` defines a workspace with members for all five services and the `crates/identity/` library crate.
* Each member exists as a compiling placeholder crate (a `main.rs`/`lib.rs` stub is sufficient) at exactly the path given in §5 — no path improvisation.
* `cargo build --workspace` and `cargo test --workspace` succeed from a clean checkout.
* Workspace-level dependency management (`[workspace.dependencies]`) is set up so shared crate versions (`tonic`, `prost`, `tokio`, `tracing`) are declared once, not per-crate.
* A `rust-toolchain.toml` pins the toolchain version.
* README documents the workspace layout and maps each crate to its service name from §5.

issues.description:
Give the shared `proto/` directory a documented structure and a versioning rule, so five service epics can add schemas in parallel without colliding or inventing five different conventions.

**Not this story:** no service's actual RPC definitions — each service epic writes its own `.proto` contents against these rules.

**Acceptance criteria**

* `proto/` has one clearly separated area per service (`gateway`, `speech`, `agent-core`, `mcp-registry`, `knowledge-core`), each with its own version segment so one can bump without forcing the others
* A convention doc in the repo fixes protobuf `package` naming, file/directory naming, the version segment format, and where cross-service shared message types may live
* The convention states what "versioned independently per service" means in practice — which changes require a new version segment and which may be made in place
* A placeholder or example schema per service area demonstrates the layout and compiles, so the structure is proven rather than only described
* The rule that a service's `.proto` is owned and edited by that service's epic is written down, including who reviews a change that affects a consumer
* The layout is exactly `proto/<service>/v1/<service>.proto` containing `package aria.<service>.v1;`, and buf's default lint and breaking-change rule sets pass against it without rule overrides

**Decisions**

* D12 — the version lives in **both** the directory and the package suffix; that is what buf's default rules expect, and ARIA-16 enforces against those rules

**Open**

* Whether any cross-service shared/common message types are permitted at all, or whether every message must belong to exactly one service's namespace

**Links:** [Decision Log — repo, proto & CI](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/decisions/0002-repo-proto-ci.md) · [Conventions](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/05-conventions.md)

issues.description:
Turn `proto/` from a folder of schema files into a real workspace crate that every service depends on for its generated client and server types.

**Not this story:** the codegen machinery only — service RPC definitions belong to their own epics.

**Acceptance criteria**

* The `proto` crate compiles every schema under `proto/` into `tonic` client + server stubs and `prost` message types, driven by the layout convention rather than a hand-maintained file list
* Adding a new `.proto` in an existing service area yields usable Rust types with at most one declarative entry, verified by actually adding a throwaway file
* A service crate consumes the generated types by depending on the `proto` crate alone; no service builds protobuf itself or reaches into `proto/` by relative path
* Generated module paths are re-exported at a stable, documented Rust path per service, so one service's version bump cannot silently rename another's types
* `protoc` availability is handled explicitly and documented (vendored/bundled vs. required on PATH), so a clean checkout builds on both a dev machine and a CI runner
* An invalid or unreachable schema fails the build loudly with a readable error rather than silently emitting nothing
* No generated `.rs` output is committed, and a clean checkout on a machine with no local `protoc` builds successfully

**Decisions**

* D14 — codegen at build time into `OUT_DIR` with `protoc` vendored and nothing generated committed; schema/codegen drift becomes impossible by construction, which is why ARIA-16 narrows to lint plus breaking-change detection

**Open**

* Which `prost` type-mapping options (`bytes` handling, well-known-type mapping, serde derives) are set workspace-wide — relevant to the streaming audio path, which is not yet designed

**Links:** [Decision Log — repo, proto & CI](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/decisions/0002-repo-proto-ci.md) · [Conventions](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/05-conventions.md)

issues.description:
Prove the whole chain — schema in `proto/`, codegen, a server, a client, a bidirectional stream — before five service epics start building against `tonic`, and leave that proof behind as the reference every service copies.

**Not this story:** the reference schema is a platform-internal test schema (e.g. an echo service), explicitly **not** a service contract and not intended to ship. The real audio channel is the Gateway epic; STT/TTS is Speech.

**Acceptance criteria**

* An integration test starts a `tonic` server, connects a client over loopback, and asserts a successful unary round-trip using types generated by the `proto` crate
* A second integration test exercises a bidirectional stream in both directions — client sends N while concurrently receiving M — proving the streaming pattern the audio channel will depend on
* Both tests run under `cargo test --workspace` with no external process, container or manual setup, so they work in CI
* The reference documents the agreed server bootstrap shape: how a service binds its listener, where interceptors/middleware attach, and how graceful shutdown is signalled
* Stream teardown is asserted, not assumed: a client dropping mid-stream and a server ending the stream early each produce a defined, tested outcome rather than a hang
* The reference is documented as copy-from-here material for service epics, with the test schema clearly marked as non-contractual
* The bootstrap uses plaintext HTTP/2 on ClusterIP with no TLS wrapping, and the docs record that in-cluster confidentiality rests on network isolation plus NetworkPolicy, together with the ARIA-79 multi-node revisit trigger

**Decisions**

* D6 — internal gRPC stays plaintext in-cluster with NetworkPolicy. **Live tripwire, not a settled answer:** if ARIA-79 reports the cluster is multi-node, voice audio crosses the LAN in plaintext and this must be revisited rather than inherited

**Open**

* Whether keepalive, message size limits and timeouts get workspace-wide defaults now or are left per-service

issues.description:
Stand up the CI skeleton that gates every change to the `aria` monorepo, so no service epic lands code on an unverified baseline. The repo is one Cargo workspace, so CI is workspace-wide by default.

**Not this story:** build/test/lint/codegen CI only. Container image build/publish and cluster deploy are Deployment & Infra — this pipeline stops at a green build.

**Acceptance criteria**

* Runs on every push and every pull request, failing the change if `cargo build --workspace`, `cargo test --workspace`, `cargo fmt --check` or `cargo clippy` fails
* Clippy warnings are denied and block the merge, rather than being advisory output nobody reads
* Uses the toolchain pinned by `rust-toolchain.toml`, so CI and local developers cannot drift onto different compiler versions
* Any system prerequisite the build needs (notably `protoc`) is installed by the pipeline itself; a clean runner succeeds with no manual step
* Cargo registry and build artifacts are cached between runs, and a cache miss still produces a correct build rather than a failure
* A deliberately broken commit (failing test, formatting violation, clippy lint) is demonstrated to turn the pipeline red
* The pipeline is a GitHub Actions workflow committed to the repository and runs on GitHub-hosted runners

**Decisions**

* D13 — GitHub Actions on GitHub-hosted runners. **Accepted trade-off:** source and build logs leave the network, narrowing local-by-default from "nothing leaves" to "no _personal_ data leaves"

**Open**

* Whether the workspace is also checked on a second target/profile (release build, `cargo deny`/audit) now or later

**Links:** [Decision Log — repo, proto & CI](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/decisions/0002-repo-proto-ci.md) · [Deployment](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/04-deployment.md)

issues.description:
Make the `proto/` conventions machine-enforced: five epics will edit schemas in the same directory, and a convention that only lives in a README will be broken within weeks. D14 narrows this story to lint plus breaking-change detection.

**Not this story:** each service epic owns the _contents_ of its own `.proto` files — this job checks them against the shared rules, it does not author them.

**Acceptance criteria**

* A schema lint runs over every file in `proto/` and fails on violations of the layout convention's naming, package and versioning rules
* A change that breaks wire compatibility within an existing service version (removing or renumbering a field, changing a type) fails CI, pointing the author at the per-service version bump
* Failures report which service area failed and why in one readable message, fixable by a contributor from another epic who does not know how codegen is wired
* The same checks are runnable locally with a single command producing identical results to CI, so failures are reproducible before pushing
* A deliberately breaking schema change is demonstrated to turn CI red
* The lint enforces the D12 layout specifically — `proto/<service>/v1/<service>.proto` containing `package aria.<service>.v1;` — which is what makes buf's default rule sets applicable without overrides

**Decisions**

* D12 — the layout the lint enforces, and the reason buf's defaults apply without rule overrides
* D14 — nothing generated is committed, so no freshness check remains to build; this story is lint plus breaking-change detection only

**Open**

* Which protobuf tooling performs lint and breaking-change detection, and whether the breaking-change baseline is the previous commit on the default branch or a published descriptor snapshot
* Whether the breaking-change gate is enforced from day one, while no service has a released schema version and every service is pre-first-deploy, or switched on at a defined point

**Links:** [Decision Log — repo, proto & CI](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/decisions/0002-repo-proto-ci.md) · [Conventions](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/05-conventions.md)

issues.description:
Make a clean checkout usable in one command, and make "it passed locally" mean the same thing as "it passed in CI". Bootstrap works at the workspace level and assumes no particular service is present.

**Acceptance criteria**

* A task runner checked into the repo exposes named tasks for at least build, test, format, lint, regenerate protobuf types, and run-all-checks — and CI invokes those same tasks rather than duplicating the command lines
* Running the all-checks task on a clean checkout reproduces the CI verdict exactly; nothing passes locally then fails CI on a check that only existed in the pipeline
* A documented bootstrap path takes a fresh machine from clone to green checks, including every non-Cargo prerequisite (notably `protoc`) and the pinned toolchain
* An optional pre-commit hook runs the fast subset (format + lint), documented as opt-in rather than silently installed
* Bootstrap docs live in the repo (README or CONTRIBUTING) and name the entry point for each of the six workspace crates, so a contributor can tell where a change belongs
* Every task works from the workspace root regardless of which subdirectory the developer is in

**Open**

* Which task runner (`just`, `cargo-make`, `make`, or plain cargo aliases) — undecided; the failure mode to avoid is two half-used runners
* Whether the same task runner is reused by MCP-server repos outside the monorepo (which can be any language) or is monorepo-only

**Links:** [Conventions](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/05-conventions.md)

issues.description:
Decide once, for all five services, how a service handles errors, loads configuration, initialises logging and lays out its tests — then write it into CLAUDE.md §7, a placeholder today.

**Not this story:** conventions and seams only. `aria-identity`'s contents belong to the Keycloak epic, `mcp-client`'s to the MCP Registry epic, OpenTelemetry instrumentation to Observability. This story defines where each plugs in.

**Acceptance criteria**

* A documented error convention maps a service's internal error type to `tonic::Status` codes at the boundary, applied in the transport reference so there is a working example
* The convention pins what may cross a service boundary in an error — conversation and voice content must not leak into logs or span attributes
* A documented config convention covers precedence (defaults, file, environment), which values are required at startup, and how a missing one fails: fast and loudly, not on first use
* Secrets and per-environment endpoints load through that same convention; no service reads an ad-hoc environment variable of its own invention
* A documented `tracing` subscriber init convention leaves the layer seam where Observability attaches OpenTelemetry, so that epic changes configuration rather than re-instrumenting
* A documented test layout convention distinguishes unit, workspace-integration and external-service tests, and states which subset must pass in CI
* CLAUDE.md §7 is updated in the same change, including the crate inventory, so it stops describing an empty repo
* The §7 fill-in records D11, D12, D14 and D23 below, and the §5 path table gains the missing `crates/mcp-client/` row

**Decisions**

* D11 — `mcp-client` lives at `crates/mcp-client/`; this story adds the placeholder crate and the §5 path-table row
* D12 — `proto/<service>/v1/<service>.proto` containing `package aria.<service>.v1;`
* D14 — build-time `OUT_DIR` codegen, nothing generated committed, `protoc` vendored
* D23 — `sqlx` with compile-time-checked queries and its migration harness

**Open**

* Which concrete error, config and logging libraries are standardised workspace-wide
* Whether config arrives as environment variables, mounted files, or Kubernetes Secrets/ConfigMaps — agree with Deployment & Infra rather than assume

comments.body:
**Decided 2026-08-19 (D47):** The ARIA client carries exactly two client roles — `aria-user` (may interact with ARIA at all) and `aria-admin` (may approve MCP servers and manage the circle) — as **client roles on the ARIA client**, not realm roles.

This closes the last "Open / needs decision" item on this story.

**Why.** The role set is much smaller than it first looks, because D7 already moved per-tool MCP permissions out of it: those live in per-MCP-server Keycloak clients as `aria:mcp:<server>:<tool>` scopes, provisioned at runtime by `aria-kc-broker` (D8). What remains for the core client is only ARIA-level authority, and at circle scale there are two kinds: people who use ARIA, and Jann. Adding a third role before a third distinction exists is ceremony — the same reasoning D5 applied to service-to-service authorization, applied consistently. Client roles rather than realm roles because the realm is shared with other homelab apps and realm roles would leak into their tokens.

**Rejected.** A third `aria-circle-manager` role splitting circle onboarding (ARIA-114) from full admin — a real distinction eventually, and it anticipates the delegation work `consent_grants.granted_by` exists for, but there is currently exactly one person who would hold either role, so the split would express nothing. A single `aria-user` role with all admin authority gated by the PR/approval path (D44) — attractively minimal and consistent with "nothing ARIA runs can approve itself", but it conflates code trust (D44's one-time gate) with runtime authority, and not every admin action routes through a PR.

**Revisit trigger.** The moment a second person needs admin-ish authority over part of ARIA but not all of it — most likely when a circle member is onboarded under ARIA-114.

Full reasoning: `docs/decisions/0009-measurement-session.md`, entry D47.

**Remaining work on this story is now purely data collection.** A fill-in template covering every fact ARIA-20/22/28/29/31 are built against — issuer, discovery URL, JWKS URI, roles claim path, the two decoded token examples, and which circle members already exist in the realm (D4) — is at `docs/spikes/ARIA-19-keycloak-facts.md`.

comments.author: FPG Schiba
comments.body:
**Hardware facts recorded 2026-08-19. The budget is PRELIMINARY — this story stays open.**

GPU node baseline established while debugging an outage (see ARIA-79 comment):

* **NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2070, 8 GB** (TU106, compute capability 7.5), driver 580.173.02 / CUDA 13.0, installed from the `.run` installer rather than Debian packages.
* Ollama runs in **LXC container CT 200** (`llm-inference`) on Proxmox `prox2`, via bind-mounted device nodes — not a VM with vfio passthrough.

**Measured footprint**, from Ollama's own memory breakdown loading `qwen3:8b`:

```
CUDA0 (RTX 2070) | 7782 MiB total | 7683 free | 5049 used = 4643 weights + 306 KV + 100 compute
```

=> **approximately 2.6 GB left for** `aria-speech` with `qwen3:8b` resident.

**Two reasons that number is not yet the published budget:**

1. **It is measured at a 4096-token context** (`OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=0`, i.e. default). ARIA's Agent Core prompt is system prompt + retrieved Knowledge Core context + the full MCP tool catalogue + conversation history, and will want considerably more. Raising context grows the KV cache and shrinks Speech's share further. The real contention is worse than the headline figure.
2. **It is at-rest, not mid-inference.** Speech's budget is what remains at the worst moment, not the average.

**Ollama configuration recorded as ARIA-managed state (D28):**

| Setting | Value | Relevance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE` | max int64 — never unloads | The single biggest lever on Speech's budget |
| `OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS` | 1 | Model swap costs a full reload — measured at 13-14 s |
| `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL` | 1 | No concurrent inference |
| `OLLAMA_KV_CACHE_TYPE` | q8_0 | Already quantised — less headroom to reclaim than it looks |
| `OLLAMA_FLASH_ATTENTION` | true | Already on |

**Non-obvious dependency, recorded because the two settings look independent and are not:** the obvious way to free VRAM for Speech is lowering `keep_alive` so Ollama unloads when idle. With GPU persistence mode **off**, that is exactly what would re-trigger the outage below — the driver can unload when no process holds the GPU, taking the device nodes with it. Ollama's infinite `keep_alive` was masking that. Persistence mode has now been enabled, which is what makes lowering `keep_alive` safe.

Still needed to close: VRAM at rest and mid-inference at ARIA's real context length, then the resident-vs-load-on-demand decision, then publish the budget for ARIA-30/ARIA-33.

Full write-up: `docs/spikes/ARIA-27-gpu-baseline.md`.

issues.description:
The primitives for the minimal signed user context that travels on every internal gRPC call: `sign()` for the Gateway to mint one, `verify()` for every other service to trust one.

**Not this story:** minting the context at the trust boundary is the Gateway epic; the key lifecycle is ARIA-113. This story owns `sign()`, `verify()`, `kid` selection and rotation overlap.

**Acceptance criteria**

* The payload carries exactly `user_id` and roles plus only what the signing mechanism requires; the type is documented as deliberately minimal, and adding a field is a reviewed decision
* `sign()`/`verify()` round-trip, and `verify()` returns a typed identity constructible nowhere else in the public API — no path from a raw `String` user id to a trusted identity, so a prompt-injected tool argument claiming to be someone else cannot become one; asserted by an API or compile-fail test
* One test each, all rejected: tampered `user_id`; tampered role list; unsigned context; unknown or wrong signing key; past the freshness window
* The context is short-lived and bound to a freshness window so a captured value cannot be replayed indefinitely; expiry is proven by a test that advances time
* Key material comes from configuration and is never committed; rotation is documented and `verify()` accepts the previous key during the overlap, proven by a test signing with the old key mid-rotation
* The wire encoding of the context is documented in one place, so the Gateway and every consumer agree without re-deriving it
* Public keys are published JWKS-style with a `kid` per key and `verify()` selects by `kid`; **two keys are live throughout a rotation**, asserted by verifying contexts signed with each against the same published key set

**Decisions**

* D1 — Ed25519: the Gateway holds the only private key and mints a short-lived JWT (`user_id`, roles, `exp`, `jti`); every other service verifies but can never mint

**Open**

* Whether the freshness window is per-request or per-session, and what value it takes — D1 fixes `exp` and `jti`, not the window's shape or value

issues.description:
Implement `src/auth.rs` — the trust boundary. Every inbound RPC must present a Keycloak-issued JWT the Gateway validates once via `aria-identity`; everything else is rejected before it reaches a handler.

**Not this story:** validation primitives, JWKS fetch/caching and the client-credentials flow live in the `aria-identity` crate (Keycloak/Identity epic). This story consumes that crate and must not reimplement validation.

**Acceptance criteria**

* A `tonic` interceptor / `tower` layer runs ahead of every RPC handler, unary and streaming alike, and delegates token validation to `aria-identity`
* Missing, malformed, expired, wrong-issuer, wrong-audience and bad-signature tokens are rejected with `UNAUTHENTICATED` and never reach a handler; one integration test per case
* For `Converse` the token is validated at stream open: an unauthenticated stream is closed before a single audio chunk is read, tested by sending chunks immediately after opening
* The raw token is never logged, never echoed into a response, and never forwarded downstream — a test asserts the credential string appears in neither captured log output nor outbound metadata
* Validated claims reach handlers through a typed request extension; no handler re-parses or re-validates the token itself
* Tokens from **both** flows on the ARIA client are accepted — Authorization Code + PKCE and the Device Authorization Grant — with an integration test per flow, so a headless device is not rejected by an assumption baked in here

**Decisions**

* D3 — one **public** client with PKCE and the Device Grant, so the interceptor must accept tokens from either flow and must not assume a confidential-client shape
* D2 — the `user_id` the Gateway lifts from the validated token is the Keycloak `sub` claim, unmodified

**Open**

* The metadata key and token-presentation convention for inbound client credentials is owned by the Keycloak/Identity epic — confirm it there rather than assuming a convention here

issues.description:
Compose the crate's primitives into the middleware services actually mount, so no service hand-rolls gRPC metadata handling or auth checks (`crates/identity/src/tower_layer.rs`; `tower` proposed).

**Not this story:** the primitives are ARIA-28 and the key lifecycle ARIA-113 — this story only mounts them.

**Acceptance criteria**

* A server-side tower `Layer`/tonic interceptor rejects — before the handler is entered — any call with no credential, an invalid or foreign service token, or a missing/invalid user context, returning `Unauthenticated` or `PermissionDenied`; a test asserts the handler is never reached in each case
* A client-side interceptor attaches the caller's service token and, when one is in scope, the signed user context, so no individual service writes metadata keys itself
* Ingress strips or overwrites any inbound user-context metadata key before egress sets its own; a forged context sent alongside a valid service token is proven not to be honoured downstream
* Handlers reach the verified identity only as a typed request extension; no accessor exposes raw unverified metadata as an identity
* Metadata key names for the service token and user context are defined once in the crate and documented, so all five services agree by construction
* Health and readiness probes are excludable only by explicit configuration; a freshly-configured layer defaults to deny
* An integration test wires two in-process tonic services through the layer: the authorised call succeeds, each unauthorised variant fails with its documented status code
* "Foreign service token" and "invalid user context" have concrete checks — a valid realm token whose `aud` names a different callee, and a context with an unknown `kid`, are each rejected by test

**Decisions**

* D1 — the context is a Gateway-minted Ed25519 JWT verified against the Gateway's JWKS by `kid`, two keys live during rotation
* D5 — a foreign token is one whose `aud` is not the mounting service's own client; no role check is needed at this layer yet

issues.description:
Turn the validated JWT into a minimal signed context (`user_id`, roles), attach it as metadata on every downstream call, and make it structurally impossible for that context to originate anywhere else — a prompt-injected message must not be able to claim to be someone else.

**Not this story:** the Gateway mints, it does not implement the primitive — `sign()`/`verify()` are ARIA-28 and the key lifecycle ARIA-113.

**Acceptance criteria**

* Every outbound gRPC call carries a context holding exactly `user_id` (the `sub` claim) and roles from the validated JWT — no other user data, no passthrough of the original token
* The context is an Ed25519-signed JWT with `exp` and `jti` set, signed with ARIA-113's key and carrying that key's `kid` so verifiers select correctly across a rotation
* The context type's constructor is private to the auth path; no request-body field, client metadata or model-produced string can populate it — enforced by construction visibility plus a test attempting the alternate paths
* A `SendCommand` whose body or metadata carries an attacker-supplied `user_id` yields a downstream call carrying the JWT-derived `user_id`; the supplied value is ignored, not merged, not preferred
* The same test exists for `Converse`, including a mid-stream message attempting to change identity after the stream opened with a valid token
* A context whose signature does not verify, or whose `exp` has passed, is rejected downstream — tested against a forged context signed with a different key
* A request without a valid JWT produces no downstream call at all; a call carrying an absent or empty context cannot be constructed — asserted by test and by the type having no default/empty value
* Roles are copied verbatim from validated claims; a token with no role claim yields an empty role set, never a default or elevated role

**Decisions**

* D1 — short-lived Ed25519-signed JWT (`user_id`, roles, `exp`, `jti`); the Gateway holds the only private key, services verify against its published JWKS, two keys live during rotation
* D2 — `user_id` is the immutable Keycloak `sub` claim, so a rename or email change does not orphan user-scoped data
* D9 — the MCP Registry separately injects a reserved `_aria_user_id` _argument_ (ARIA-82); that is contextual identity, never used for enforcement — enforcement reads only the signed metadata minted here

issues.description:
**RESOLVED 2026-08-12 by decision D7.** This spike is closed; no investigation remains.

**Decided:** one Keycloak scope per **tool**, not per server, named `aria:mcp:<server-slug>:<tool>`. The `aria:` prefix prevents collision in the realm ARIA shares with other homelab apps — Keycloak scope names are realm-global, and CLAUDE.md's originally-suggested `mcp:<server-name>` would have claimed a namespace ARIA does not own. Slug and tool charset are fixed at registration so a server name cannot produce an invalid or colliding scope.

**Why per-tool rather than per-server:** it puts individual tools in front of Keycloak's own consent screen and account-console revocation, so a user can see and revoke a single capability through a surface that already exists.

**Rejected:** `mcp:<server-name>` (namespace collision in a shared realm); a per-server scope with per-tool granularity living only in `consent_grants` (needs no Keycloak write on tool drift and treats remote LAN servers identically, but keeps per-tool visibility out of Keycloak's revocation UI).

**Cost accepted deliberately.** Keycloak scopes end up roughly 1:1 with `consent_grants` rows, and tool-list drift now requires a Keycloak write. That consequence forced decision **D8** — runtime scope provisioning through the new `aria-kc-broker` service (ARIA-110), because remote LAN servers never pass through the deploy pipeline.

Full reasoning and rejected alternatives: **ARIA — Decision Log**, entry D7. Current state: CLAUDE.md §2 (Consent & permissions) and the **ARIA — Observability, Identity & Consent** page.

**Consumers:** ARIA-38, ARIA-68, ARIA-70, ARIA-75, ARIA-88, ARIA-90, ARIA-110.

issues.description:
Implement `src/audio.rs` and the `Converse` handler in `src/grpc/interface.rs`: accept an inbound audio chunk stream, frame and buffer it, forward it downstream, and stream responses back on the same connection while the client is still sending.

**Not this story:** STT and TTS are the Speech epic — this story owns audio **transport** only, no processing or model invocation. Stopping Speech triggering on ARIA's own synthesised voice (echo cancellation, or half-duplex gating as a cheaper substitute) is ARIA-116.

**Acceptance criteria**

* One stream: a client sends N audio chunks and receives responses on it while still sending — proven by a test that interleaves send and receive rather than sending everything first
* Inbound chunks reassemble to the downstream frame size without loss or reordering: a known byte sequence streamed in irregular, non-frame-aligned chunks reconstructs byte-identically at the downstream boundary
* The context established at stream open attaches to every downstream call for that session and no mid-stream client message can alter it — test asserts the downstream `user_id` is constant and JWT-derived for the stream's lifetime
* An abrupt mid-stream disconnect releases all Gateway-side resources for that session (task, buffers, downstream stream) within a bounded time; repeated abrupt disconnects show no task or memory growth
* No audio bytes are written to disk or emitted to logs — only chunk counts and sizes are observable
* The client link carries Opus in 20 ms frames, decoded to mono s16le PCM before forwarding to Speech; the reassembly test runs against that frame size
* One `Converse` stream carries many turns, and utterance boundaries arrive as events from Speech rather than being inferred here
* A speech-start signal from Speech during outbound synthesis cancels that session's outbound TTS stream within a bounded, tested time

**Decisions**

* D25 — Opus on the client link, PCM internally; the decode hop is the Gateway's
* D26 — Speech owns VAD and endpointing, so the Gateway stays pure transport, at the accepted cost of audio streaming to the cluster during silence
* D27 — one stream carries many turns and barge-in is supported, which is why cancelling the outbound TTS stream is a criterion here

**Open**

* The exact model-facing sample rate — D25 left it to ARIA-30 rather than asserting it here

issues.description:
Make the audio channel survive a fast producer and a slow consumer without unbounded memory growth, and make every way a session can end release the same resources — a Gateway pod must be killable and restartable at any moment without leaking or wedging.

**Not this story:** external/remote access and any ingress-level rate limiting, both explicitly deferred.

**Acceptance criteria**

* Buffers between the inbound stream and the downstream consumer are bounded; a load test with a producer faster than the consumer shows Gateway memory stabilising rather than growing without limit

* Configurable per-stream limits — maximum concurrent `Converse` streams, maximum session duration, idle timeout with no chunks received — are enforced, and breaching one returns a defined gRPC status (e.g. `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED`) rather than hanging the client
* Teardown is symmetric: client-initiated close, Gateway-initiated close and downstream failure each release the identical set of resources; a repeated open/close cycle test shows no task, socket or memory leak
* Every stream termination records a reason code, so an operator can distinguish client hang-up from idle timeout from load shed from downstream failure

**Open**

* The actual limit values — concurrent stream cap, idle timeout, maximum session length. ARIA serves one person plus a small circle rather than multi-tenant SaaS, so the numbers can be small, but none is specified

issues.description:
Decision spike choosing the provider and model behind the Agent Core's default backend. No production code ships beyond throwaway probes. ARIA serves one person plus a small circle, so scale is not the driver — tool-calling reliability and cost are.

**Not this story:** provisioning the API credential and writing the egress rules — both belong to Deployment & Infra; this spike hands them the contract.

**Acceptance criteria**

* A written comparison of at least two candidate providers/models covering, per candidate: tool-calling reliability, whether multiple tool calls can be returned in one response, streaming support, request/response schema shape, rate limits, and rough cost per typical ARIA request
* Each candidate exercised with a throwaway probe on a representative ARIA prompt carrying at least five MCP-style tool schemas; observed tool-selection behaviour and malformed-tool-call rate recorded as measured evidence, not asserted from documentation
* The adapter mapping the chosen provider's tool-call format into ARIA's canonical type is specified for `src/llm/hosted.rs` — per D49 an adapter is required either way, since no vendor's wire format becomes the internal shape
* The single outbound host/port the service will contact is documented, so the Deployment epic can write egress rules — only the hosted LLM call leaves the network
* How the API credential reaches the service (env var name / secret key name) is specified as a contract; the provisioning mechanism is left to Deployment & Infra
* The outcome — chosen provider and model, rejected alternatives and why — is written back to the Agent Core page and the open-questions list before this story closes

**Decisions**

* D49 — the canonical internal tool-call shape is ARIA's own, deliberately modelled close to OpenAI's; both the hosted and Ollama backends adapt _into_ it, so ARIA-50's conformance suite cannot quietly become a test of one vendor

comments.author: FPG Schiba
comments.body:
**Decided 2026-08-19 (D49): the canonical internal tool-call shape is ARIA's own.**

This resolves one of this story's acceptance criteria — "whether the chosen provider's tool-call format becomes the internal canonical shape or whether an adapter layer is required" — **ahead of** the provider choice itself, because the answer turns out not to depend on it.

**Decided.** An **ARIA-owned type**, deliberately modelled close to the OpenAI tool-call shape. Both the hosted backend and the Ollama backend adapt _into_ it. No vendor's wire format becomes ARIA's internal type.

**Why.** ARIA-50 requires a backend-agnostic conformance suite that both backends pass unmodified, and D35 makes the Ollama fallback non-optional. If a vendor's format were canonical, the other backend would permanently translate into a foreign shape and the conformance suite would quietly become a test of that vendor.

**The counter-argument was measured away.** The case for adopting OpenAI's shape verbatim was that Ollama exposes an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, making one adapter nearly free. Probing on 2026-08-19 removed that saving: **Ollama's OpenAI-compatible endpoint cannot disable a model's thinking phase** — `think: false` exists only on the native `/api/chat` — and thinking models reason before emitting a tool call, which with five tool schemas in the prompt exceeded a 120 s timeout in practice. The Ollama backend needs the native endpoint regardless, so **neither adapter is free** and the saving that justified vendor-shaped canonicalisation does not exist.

**Rejected.** _OpenAI's shape verbatim_ — one adapter nearly free and it is the de-facto interchange format, but it makes ARIA-50's suite vendor-flavoured and the measured constraint above undercuts the saving. _Deferring to ARIA-50_ — costs nothing today, but ARIA-53 and ARIA-54 both inherit the answer, and leaving it implicit is how a vendor shape becomes canonical by accident.

**Two new requirements this creates:**

* **ARIA-54** — the Ollama backend must set the thinking parameter **explicitly** rather than inherit the model's default.
* **ARIA-61** — the tool-loop latency budget must account for a reasoning phase the hosted path does not have.

**Open, and now measured separately:** whether tool arguments arrive **fragmented** (OpenAI streams them as partial strings needing accumulation) or **complete** (Ollama sends whole objects). This is an adapter difference the `LlmBackend` trait must absorb. The probe harness now measures it under `--stream`.

**Still open on this story:** the provider and model themselves (the harness is ready — `scripts/aria-llm-probe.py`, run with `--provider anthropic|gemini|openai`), and the OpenAI model IDs and pricing, which could not be sourced from OpenAI's own page in this session and should not be taken from an aggregator.

**Settled and unchanged:** egress is a single HTTPS/443 host, allow-listed per provider; the credential contract is the env var `ARIA_LLM_API_KEY` from a sealed secret (D31) with key `llm-api-key`, deliberately provider-neutral so switching provider is a config change not a manifest change.

Full reasoning: `docs/decisions/0009-measurement-session.md` entry D49, and `docs/spikes/ARIA-40-hosted-llm-backend.md`.

comments.author: FPG Schiba
comments.body:
**Decided 2026-08-19 (D50):** `aria-speech` asserts GPU availability at startup and fails closed.

The service verifies it can reach the GPU at startup and **refuses to become ready** without it, rather than falling back to CPU and serving degraded. This is a new acceptance criterion for this story (the assertion belongs in the scaffold's startup path); ARIA-93 carries the deployment-side half (the readiness probe must reflect it).

**Why — this is not hypothetical, it was observed.** On 2026-08-19, after a Proxmox host power-cycle, Ollama on the GPU node ran **100% on CPU while appearing entirely healthy**: API responsive, models listed, generation roughly 50x too slow. Root cause was an LXC bind mount silently creating empty regular files instead of device nodes, suppressed by `bind,optional,create=file`.

A pod that starts, passes its health check and runs 50x too slow **pages nobody**. On a voice path that degradation is the difference between a usable assistant and one nobody uses — but it produces no signal a monitoring system would catch. A crash is strictly better than a silent capability loss, because a crash is actionable.

**Rejected.** _Warn loudly but keep serving_ — "degraded speech beats no speech" is a real argument for a household assistant and is what most services do, but it requires the alerting question (deferred as C-5) to be answered first, and warning into a log nobody reads is exactly how the incident above went unnoticed. _Also dropping_ `bind,optional` from the LXC mounts so the container refuses to start — belt-and-braces and arguably correct for a host named `llm-inference`, but that is a host-configuration choice on shared homelab infrastructure rather than an ARIA service decision; recorded as an open item instead.

**Consequence for the deferred alerting question (C-5).** It was deferred on the grounds that there is "nothing to alert on until services run". This incident is a counter-example that already happened: a silent capability loss with no signal. C-5 should be revisited when Speech is deployed, not when services first run.

**Related preliminary facts for this epic** (`docs/spikes/ARIA-27-gpu-baseline.md`): the GPU is an **RTX 2070, 8 GB**; roughly **2.6 GB** remains with `qwen3:8b` resident, measured at a 4096-token context and at rest. That is not yet a published budget — ARIA-27 still needs the mid-inference figure at ARIA's real context length. Note also that Ollama reaches the GPU through an **LXC bind mount on Proxmox**, not a Kubernetes device plugin, so whether there is a k8s-visible GPU resource for this pod to request at all is an open question owned by ARIA-79.

Full reasoning: `docs/decisions/0009-measurement-session.md`, entry D50.

issues.description:
**Scope changed 2026-08-12 (D16) — this is still an open spike, but it is no longer the same spike.** The embed-vs-structured split for preferences is settled: typed preferences are authoritative in Postgres, free-text preferences are authoritative in Qdrant. What this spike must now produce is the **classification rule** — how to decide which kind a given preference is, and what happens when one changes kind — rather than a list of what gets embedded. It must also record the consequence that Qdrant now holds primary data and is not rebuildable from Postgres. See the Decided and Open blocks at the foot of this issue.

## Context

CLAUDE.md §8 lists this as an open question:

> "Design the Knowledge Core retrieval step: what's embedded into Qdrant vs. kept as structured Postgres attributes, and what write permissions a connected MCP service has into it."

That is genuinely two decisions. **This story covers the first half only** — the embed-vs-structured split. The write-permission half is a separate spike.

CLAUDE.md §2 assigns the two stores:

> "**Postgres** (structured: social graph, preferences-as-attributes, MCP server registry, calendar) + **Qdrant** (semantic: embeddings of facts, preferences, conversation history)."

Note that _preferences_ appear on both sides of that row. Resolving that overlap is the core of this spike.

## Acceptance criteria

* A written decision record (in-repo ADR or Confluence page, linked from this issue) classifies every known knowledge category — people, relationships, preferences, calendar entries, learned facts, conversation history — as structured-only, embedded-only, or dual-stored.
* For every dual-stored category the record names the authoritative store and specifies how the embedded copy is regenerated when the structured row changes (including deletes).
* The record defines the payload/metadata carried alongside each Qdrant vector — at minimum the owning `user_id`, the source, and a reference back to the structured row where one exists — so retrieval results are traceable into Postgres.
* The record states how a retrieval result set is scoped to one person, honouring §2: "Every service that touches user data operates against an explicit `user_id` — there is no implicit 'current user.'"
* Reviewed with the Agent Core epic owner (the consumer of retrieval) before this is closed; anything still unresolved is written down as an open item rather than assumed.
* No production code is delivered beyond throwaway prototypes used to inform the decision.
* The record states the **classification rule** that decides whether a given preference is typed (Postgres-authoritative) or free-text (Qdrant-authoritative), and what happens to a preference that changes kind after it has already been stored (D16).
* The record states which categories are primary data in Qdrant and therefore not re-derivable from Postgres, so backup and restore (ARIA-96) can act on that list (D16).

## Out of scope

* When retrieval is invoked and how a prompt is assembled — Agent Core owns that.
* The choice of embedding model/provider — separate spike.

**Decided 2026-08-12 (D16):** preferences are split by kind rather than by precedence — structured, typed preferences (`timezone=Europe/Zurich`, units, quiet hours) are authoritative in Postgres, free-text preferences ("I like my coffee strong") are authoritative in Qdrant, and no preference lives in both as a peer, so there is no dual-write and no "which store wins" question. Chosen because the two kinds genuinely are different data: a typed attribute wants exact lookup and constraints, while a fuzzy preference is only ever used through semantic retrieval, so round-tripping it through a Postgres row adds nothing. Rejected: _Postgres authoritative with Qdrant purely derived_, which would have given one system of record and a fully rebuildable index, at the cost of storing free-text preferences somewhere they are never read from directly; and _genuine dual-write_, the state the document was accidentally in, which has no consistency story at all. **Consequence, recorded because it is not free: Qdrant now holds primary data — it is no longer a rebuildable index and cannot be regenerated from Postgres.** Full reasoning: **ARIA — Decision Log**, entry D16.

**Open / needs decision:** the classification rule itself, which is now this spike's output. D16 fixes _that_ preferences are partitioned by kind; it does not say how to decide which kind a given preference is, nor what happens when one changes kind after the fact. The classification of the remaining knowledge categories listed in the acceptance criteria above is likewise still open, and downstream stories must not pre-empt either answer. Also newly open from D16: whether there is a reconciliation or merge order when a typed and a free-text preference conflict, since any read that assembles a full picture of a person now queries both stores.

comments.author: FPG Schiba
comments.body:
**Decided 2026-08-19 (D48): the classification rule this spike exists to produce.**

A preference is **typed** (authoritative in Postgres) if and only if all three hold:

1. **A closed value domain exists** — enumerable or constrained (IANA timezone, unit system, an `HH:MM` range, a boolean, an enum).
2. **Something reads it by exact lookup**, not by similarity — code asks "what is X's timezone?" and needs _the_ answer, not the three nearest.
3. **Being wrong is a bug, not a nuance** — a wrong timezone fires an alarm at the wrong hour.

**Everything else is free-text** (authoritative in Qdrant). **Free-text is the default**; promoting something to typed is a deliberate act that adds a column and a constraint.

**Kind changes are a migration, never a dual-write.** Free-text → typed: write the Postgres row, _then_ delete the Qdrant point, in that order — a crash between the two leaves a recoverable duplicate, while the reverse order loses data. Typed → free-text is the same shape reversed and should involve a human. The moment a preference exists in both stores as a peer, D16's "no consistency story" problem is back.

**On conflict, typed wins** on any fact the typed schema can express. The typed store only ever holds facts someone deliberately promoted, so a conflicting free-text point is stale by construction — flag it for cleanup, do not merge.

**Why free-text as the default matters more than the test itself:** it makes the failure mode of an unclassified fact "retrievable but fuzzy" rather than "silently dropped". The test is deliberately about value domains and read patterns, both properties of the data — which is why this was decidable now and did **not** need to wait on ARIA-52's embedding model.

**Rejected.** _Typed as the default_ — safer for correctness, but forces schema to be invented for things only ever read by similarity, which is the overbuilding D16 walked away from. _Deferring until ARIA-52_ — superficially cautious, but the embedder has no bearing on whether a fact has a closed value domain.

**Qdrant-primary category list, now publishable for ARIA-96:** **free-text preferences** and **learned facts**. These are primary data under D16 and must be backed up as sources of truth, not as a rebuildable index. Everything else (people, relationships, typed preferences, calendar cache, conversation history, registry/consent/audit tables) is Postgres-authoritative.

**Still open on this story:** whether conversation history additionally gets a _derived_ Qdrant index for retrieval. D36 makes Postgres authoritative for it, so such an index would be the one legitimately rebuildable collection — a different pattern from the two primary ones, and it should be decided explicitly rather than drift into existence.

Full reasoning and the Qdrant payload contract (`owner_user_id` as a **filter**, not a post-hoc check; `source`, `kind`, `person_id`, timestamps): `docs/decisions/0009-measurement-session.md` entry D48, and `docs/spikes/ARIA-43-knowledge-classification.md`.

comments.author: FPG Schiba
comments.body:
**Closing 2026-08-19.** The classification rule this spike existed to produce is decided as **D48**, and every acceptance criterion is met. Full record: `docs/decisions/0009-measurement-session.md` (D48) and `docs/spikes/ARIA-43-knowledge-classification.md`.

| Criterion | Outcome |
| --- | --- |
| Classify every known knowledge category | People/relationships → Postgres. Typed preferences → Postgres. **Free-text preferences → Qdrant.** **Learned facts → Qdrant.** Calendar occurrences → Postgres (a mirror, D20). Conversation history → Postgres (D36). Registry/consent/audit tables → Postgres |
| For dual-stored categories: authoritative store + regeneration | **None are dual-stored** — that is the point of D16's partition-by-kind, and D48 keeps it that way. A kind change is a **migration in a fixed order** (write the new store, then delete the old), never a dual-write |
| Payload/metadata alongside each Qdrant vector | `owner_user_id` (D18), `source` (D21), `kind`, `person_id` where one exists, `created_at`/`updated_at` — the last pair because retention (X10) cannot be implemented without them |
| How a retrieval result set is scoped to one person | `owner_user_id` filters **in Qdrant's filter clause**, never as a post-hoc discard. A post-filter still ranks another person's facts against the query, leaking through relevance scores and result counts even when payloads are dropped |
| Reviewed with the Agent Core epic owner | Reviewed and accepted by Jann, 2026-08-19 |
| No production code | None delivered |
| The classification rule, and what happens on a kind change | **D48:** typed only if a closed value domain exists **and** it is read by exact lookup **and** being wrong is a bug. **Free-text is the default.** On conflict, **typed wins**; the stale free-text point is flagged, not merged |
| Which categories are primary data in Qdrant, for ARIA-96 | **Free-text preferences and learned facts.** These are not rebuildable from Postgres and must be backed up as sources of truth |

**Two things carried forward rather than closed here:**

* **Whether conversation history additionally gets a _derived_ Qdrant index for retrieval.** D36 makes Postgres authoritative for it, so such an index would be the one legitimately rebuildable collection — a different pattern from the two primary ones. Tracked in `docs/open-questions/needs-decision.md`; not a criterion of this story.
* **The embedding model remains ARIA-52's**, blocked on ARIA-27. Note the constraint the brief surfaced: a **hosted** embedding API would be a _fourth_ thing crossing the network boundary and would ship knowledge-base content out, which §4's posture does not permit. This is effectively a choice among **self-hostable** models unless that boundary is deliberately widened — and worth testing CPU-only candidates (Nomic, BGE-M3) first, since that would remove GPU contention from the question entirely.

issues.description:
**RESOLVED 2026-08-12 by decision D35.** This spike is closed.

**Decided:** the hosted API remains the default. Ollama takes over on **error or timeout**. An explicit per-request or config-level **override** can force the local backend. **No automatic task-class routing yet.**

**Why the answer stops there.** Task-class routing — send simple turns local, tool-orchestration turns hosted — needs a quality threshold, and the measurement that would set it does not exist. The local model's actual tool-calling reliability had never been measured, and was in fact buried inside ARIA-54 rather than owned by any spike. A routing policy resting on an unmeasured quality assumption is exactly the invented certainty this backlog was built to avoid. The explicit override still provides a lever without pretending to a policy.

**Rejected:** task-class routing now (real cost and privacy gains for everyday turns, but rests on an unmeasured assumption); failover only with no override (nothing to get wrong, but the GPU capacity CLAUDE.md §2 explicitly wanted to use would sit idle outside outages, with no lever at all).

**Revisit trigger — this decision is deliberately reopenable.** ARIA-109 now measures candidate Ollama models' tool-calling reliability against the conformance suite. Once that lands, automatic routing becomes decidable and this should be reopened rather than inherited as settled.

Full reasoning: **ARIA — Decision Log**, entry D35. Current state: CLAUDE.md §2 (Agent Core "brain").

A developer-only CLI that opens a `Converse` stream, pushes audio chunks from a file or a synthetic generator, and prints responses as they arrive. **Acceptance criteria**

* The harness lives on the Gateway crate's dev/test surface (example or dev-dependency-only binary) and is absent from the shipped `aria-gateway` release artifact — verified by a build producing the service binary without it
* It opens a `Converse` stream against a running Gateway using a supplied Keycloak token, streams a WAV/raw file or a synthetic tone as chunks, and prints returned messages as they arrive rather than only at stream end

issues.description:
Where the epic's hardest constraint gets enforced in code. `aria-speech` is a guest on a GPU Ollama already occupies: it must load within the measured ceiling, notice when headroom disappears, and refuse work rather than trigger an out-of-memory that takes Ollama down with it.

**Not this story:** the PVC object itself is Deployment & Infra's — this story owns what lands on the volume and how the service loads it.

**Acceptance criteria**

* STT and TTS weights load from the configured PVC-mounted path; a missing, truncated or checksum-mismatched file gives a named readiness failure, never a mid-request panic
* A documented procedure repopulates the PVC from scratch: which files, from where, verified by checksum
* Steady-state VRAM under the chosen residency policy measured **with the Ollama model resident**, under the VRAM-budget ceiling, with the headroom recorded on the issue
* An admission guard refuses new `Transcribe`/`Synthesize` streams with the contract's gRPC status when free VRAM is below the configured reserve, instead of attempting the allocation; tested by squeezing free VRAM on the node
* A configurable limit on simultaneous streams is enforced, and behaviour past it (reject vs queue) matches the contract
* The chosen residency policy's cost is measured: cold-start load time per model if on demand, idle VRAM occupancy if resident
* A soak run of repeated streams — and repeated load/unload cycles if on demand — shows no VRAM growth from start to finish
* The Ollama-side settings the VRAM guarantee depends on (residency, concurrency, preloading) are recorded as ARIA-managed configuration, so the headroom figure is reproducible against a known Ollama configuration

**Decisions**

* D28 — ARIA may change Ollama's server configuration, not merely per-request parameters. **Accepted cost:** Ollama's configuration becomes ARIA-managed state, and a change made for Speech affects everything else using that GPU

**Open**

* Whether models stay resident or load on demand — the VRAM-budget and model spikes decide it; D28 gives a lever over Ollama's side of the budget but does not settle this
* Size of the free-VRAM reserve at which the admission guard trips
* Behaviour when Ollama grows its own footprint mid-session: evict ARIA's models, degrade to CPU, or fail requests — D28 adds reconfiguring Ollama as a further option, but which is chosen is still open
* Whether STT and TTS models load/unload independently or always move together

issues.description:
**RESOLVED 2026-08-12 by decisions D21 and D22.** This spike is closed.

**Decided — two rules together (D21).** Every Knowledge Core row carries a `source` identifying the server that wrote it, and **a server may only modify rows it authored**. Separately, the KC _areas_ a server may touch (`memory:write`, `people:read`, …) are **declared at registration and fixed by the approval gate**.

**Why.** This delivers the vision's "extendable by every connected MCP service" without letting a Sonos controller rewrite the social graph. Per-row provenance also means a wrong fact can be attributed to whoever wrote it — which matters most for servers ARIA generated herself.

**Decided — where it is enforced (D22).** The **Knowledge Core validates writes itself**, checking the calling service's identity from its own client-credentials token rather than trusting the MCP Registry's gate. Without this, any service with network access to the KC bypasses every consent and permission check, leaving NetworkPolicy as the only barrier. Accepted cost: the rule is implemented in two places and must not drift.

**Rejected:** no direct writes at all, with only the Agent Core writing (simplest and safest, one writer and one provenance story — but it contradicts the vision and makes the Agent Core a bottleneck for everything learned); capability scopes without source ownership (less schema overhead, but two servers can silently overwrite each other and nothing is attributable).

Full reasoning: **ARIA — Decision Log**, entries D21 and D22. Current state: CLAUDE.md §2/§3 and the **ARIA — Knowledge Core** page.

**Consumers:** ARIA-55, ARIA-59, ARIA-62, ARIA-68, ARIA-76, ARIA-108, ARIA-120.

issues.description:
Stand up the service skeleton and the one RPC the Gateway calls. Proposed layout (not decided): `services/agent-core/` with `main.rs`, `config.rs`, `grpc/mod.rs`, on `tonic` and `tracing`.

**Acceptance criteria**

* `services/agent-core/` exists in the `aria` monorepo as crate `aria-agent-core`; it builds and tests in the shared Cargo workspace
* This epic's `.proto` declares `Decide` and is generated through the shared `proto/` codegen, so the Gateway compiles a client with no hand-written stub
* The `tonic` server starts, serves `Decide` end to end with a stub response, and exposes a health/readiness endpoint suitable for k3s probes; the service is stateless and pins to no node
* `config.rs` loads and validates every downstream endpoint (Knowledge Core, MCP Registry, hosted LLM, Ollama) and secret at startup; a missing or malformed required value fails startup with a named error, not at first request
* Every `Decide` call opens a `tracing` span carrying the propagated `user_id`; a test asserts no raw credential or bearer token reaches a span field or log line
* The handler verifies the propagated identity context via `aria-identity` and rejects calls without a valid one; an integration test proves a missing or tampered context is refused before any LLM, retrieval or tool path runs
* `Decide` is declared **server-streaming** and its request message carries the Gateway-minted `session_id`, so the request message can be frozen
* No MCP SDK dependency (e.g. `rmcp`); the only path to MCP servers is the generated gRPC client for the MCP Registry

**Decisions**

* D36 — the Gateway mints the `session_id`; the Agent Core owns that session's history and persists it to the Knowledge Core (new schema work, ARIA-115), which is what D29's reconnect resumes into
* D37 — `Decide` streams text chunks and tool-call events, never one complete response
* D38 — no MCP SDK; tool schemas cross the Registry boundary as JSON Schema in the proto, so the `rmcp` dependency on the Agent Core page is an error

issues.description:
The real decoding pipeline behind the `Transcribe` RPC, wired to the model chosen in the STT spike. Audio arrives as a stream, so transcription must work incrementally rather than waiting for a complete file.

**Not this story:** preventing ARIA's own synthesised voice from triggering VAD — echo cancellation, or half-duplex gating as a cheaper substitute — is ARIA-116. This story implements listening-during-synthesis and the speech-start signal, not the self-triggering problem.

**Acceptance criteria**

* `Transcribe` consumes chunked audio and emits partial hypotheses while audio is still arriving, then exactly one final transcript at end-of-stream, matching the contract's partial/final distinction
* Time-to-first-partial and end-of-speech-to-final-transcript latency measured on the GPU node **with the Ollama model resident**, recorded as the no-regression baseline
* Accuracy on the fixed reference audio set matches the STT spike's figure within a stated tolerance
* A client that disconnects or cancels mid-stream aborts the decode and releases the decoder slot and any GPU memory within a bounded, tested time
* Malformed, unsupported-format or out-of-declared-order audio frames return the contract's gRPC status and terminate the stream cleanly instead of stalling
* The response carries transcribed text only — no intent, no command parsing, no dialogue state
* `Transcribe` consumes mono s16le PCM and needs no language selection in the request
* This service decides when the speaker stopped and emits utterance-boundary events upstream; the caller never signals end-of-utterance
* Transcription keeps running while a synthesised response plays on the same session and emits a speech-start signal when the user talks over ARIA, so the Gateway can cancel the outbound TTS stream — detection latency measured
* No transcript — final or partial — is persisted or written to a log line at any level; a test asserts a marked utterance produces no occurrence in this service's output or on its filesystem
* The debug capture mode is off by default, time-boxed, writes to a known path, logs loudly while active, and is asserted disabled in the deployed configuration

**Decisions**

* D24 — English only: no language field in the request, no auto-detection, one model loaded
* D25 — the Gateway decodes the client's Opus, so input is mono s16le PCM; the exact sample rate is ARIA-30's output
* D26 — endpointing/VAD lives here, not in the client or Gateway. **Accepted cost:** audio streams to the cluster during silence — cheap on a LAN, revisit if external access is designed
* D27 — one stream carries many turns with barge-in, so decoding must continue during synthesis
* D56 — Speech is stateless with respect to text: no transcript persisted or logged at any level, partials never persisted at all, with one off-by-default time-boxed capture mode as the named exception

**Open**

* Whether partial hypotheses are emitted on a timer, on decoder-stable output, or per chunk

issues.description:
The single interface both LLM backends sit behind — the story that makes "pluggable" real. Proposed home `src/llm/mod.rs`, `serde_json` tool-call schemas. Both implementations are blocked by this story and land in the same arc of work; neither is a later phase.

**Acceptance criteria**

* `src/llm/mod.rs` defines an async `LlmBackend` trait covering at minimum: submitting assembled context plus the current tool list, receiving either a final text answer or one-or-more tool calls, and submitting tool results back for the next turn
* Tool schemas and calls use one provider-neutral `serde_json` shape; provider-specific serialisation stays inside the backend, and no type outside `src/llm/` names a provider or a provider-specific field
* A structured error type separates retryable failures (timeout, rate limit, 5xx) from non-retryable ones (auth, malformed request), so failover can branch without string matching
* A shared conformance suite runs one case list against any implementation — plain answer, single tool call, multiple tool calls in one response, tool-result round-trip, malformed model output, backend error — and gates both `hosted.rs` and `ollama.rs`
* A mock in-memory `LlmBackend` lets retrieval, tool-loop and `Decide` tests run deterministically with no network
* A compile- or test-time check shows a third backend needs only a trait implementation, with no change to `grpc/`, `retrieval.rs` or `tools.rs`
* The trait is **streaming**: it yields text chunks and tool-call events incrementally, not one complete response
* The suite also covers streaming and **interleaved tool-call events** — tool calls arriving between partial text chunks — and is run by ARIA-109 against candidate Ollama models
* The trait carries multi-turn message history, since the Agent Core owns it per `session_id`; the concrete message shape is this story's own output

**Decisions**

* D37 — server-streaming `Decide` sets this trait's signature; accepted cost is a more complex trait and tool loop
* D36 — the Agent Core owns per-`session_id` history, so the trait carries it; the shape is this story's output, not a blocked dependency
