issues.description:
The TTS half of the service. ARIA is voice-first, so the gap between the assistant having words and the user hearing them is a primary quality attribute: synthesis must start emitting audio before the whole utterance is rendered.

**Not this story:** preventing ARIA's own synthesised voice from triggering VAD — echo cancellation or half-duplex gating — is ARIA-116.

**Acceptance criteria**

* `Synthesize` accepts text and streams audio chunks back, the first chunk emitted before synthesis of the full utterance completes; verified by a client measuring request to first byte of audio
* Time-to-first-audio-chunk and synthesis real-time factor measured on the GPU node **with the Ollama model resident**, recorded as the regression baseline
* Cancelling mid-synthesis stops the work and releases the slot and any GPU memory within a bounded, tested time
* A multi-sentence paragraph synthesises without truncation or audible discontinuity at chunk boundaries; input over the configured maximum returns the contract's gRPC status rather than being silently cut short
* Emitted audio's sample rate, channel count and encoding match what the response message declares, and a reference client plays the stream back with no format-negotiation guesswork
* The voice/model is the one confirmed in the TTS spike, loaded from the PVC-mounted path — no weights in the repo or the image
* A text-normalisation step runs ahead of synthesis: the library's built-in handling used unchanged where adequate, and every ARIA-specific rule justified by a recorded case the library got wrong
* Barge-in cancellation is exercised as a routine path, not only as a client hang-up: a cancel arriving mid-utterance because the user started speaking stops audio within the bounded time above and leaves the session able to serve the next turn

**Decisions**

* D30 — text normalisation lives in this service, starting from the chosen library's own handling, with ARIA-specific rules added only where it demonstrably fails; this closes the gap where no epic owned it
* D27 — barge-in makes mid-stream cancellation a normal, frequent path here rather than only a hang-up case

**Open**

* **Wire format of synthesised audio** (encoding, sample rate, chunk size) — undecided, settled jointly with the proto contract story
* Whether input is plain text only or supports markup/SSML for emphasis, pauses and pronunciation; if supported it is a pass-through, since authoring such markup would edge toward the NLG this project excludes
* Whether more than one voice is selectable per request

issues.description:
Implements `src/llm/hosted.rs`, the default backend, over `reqwest` with `serde_json` tool schemas. Ships in the same arc as the Ollama backend rather than ahead of it.

**Acceptance criteria**

* `src/llm/hosted.rs` implements `LlmBackend` against the provider and model chosen by the provider spike, and passes the shared conformance suite with no case skipped or marked provider-specific
* Tool schemas translate from the neutral shape into the provider's tool-calling format and the model's calls back, including more than one tool call in a single response
* The API credential is read from config only; a test asserts it never appears in a log line, tracing field, error message or `Debug` output
* Timeouts, bounded retries and backoff are implemented, and every failure maps onto the trait's retryable/non-retryable taxonomy so failover acts without inspecting HTTP details
* The outbound request carries only the context the Agent Core assembled — no Keycloak JWT, no propagated identity metadata, no service credential
* Per-request latency and token usage, where the provider reports it, are emitted as tracing fields so cost can be observed later
* The provider's streaming response is surfaced as incremental text chunks and tool-call events through the trait; the suite's streaming and interleaved-tool-call cases pass
* The credential is a sealed secret decrypted in-cluster and mounted as an ordinary Kubernetes Secret; nothing in this crate handles the plaintext key outside config loading

**Decisions**

* D37 — the backend must stream rather than await a complete response, because `Decide` is server-streaming
* D31 — the API key arrives as a sealed secret; sealing needs only the cluster's public certificate, so with GitHub-hosted runners (D13) no private key ever leaves the network

**Open**

* The provider and model themselves come from ARIA-40; do not hardcode a choice ahead of it

issues.description:
Implements `src/llm/ollama.rs`, the fallback backend, over `reqwest` against the Ollama instance already running on the GPU node. Delivered alongside the hosted backend behind the same trait, not as a follow-up to it.

**Not this story:** wiring a client to the existing endpoint. Deploying Ollama, and the server-side reconfiguration D28 permits, land in the deployment stories (ARIA-81, ARIA-93).

**Acceptance criteria**

* `src/llm/ollama.rs` implements `LlmBackend` over `reqwest` against Ollama's existing REST endpoint, with host and model name from `config.rs` — neither hardcoded
* It passes the identical conformance suite used for `hosted.rs`, with no case skipped, weakened or annotated "hosted-only"
* Tool calls translate between Ollama's representation and the neutral shape; a malformed or non-conforming tool call from the local model surfaces as a typed error, never silently dropped or partially executed
* Failures map onto the same retryable/non-retryable taxonomy as the hosted backend, so the selection layer treats both uniformly
* An integration test runs against the real Ollama instance or a recorded fixture, and documents which mode it ran in
* All Ollama traffic stays inside the homelab network — a test or review check confirms this path adds no outbound internet egress
* The model name stays a pure config value with no default baked into the code, so ARIA-109's outcome can be adopted without a code change

**Decisions**

* D35 — hosted stays the default and Ollama takes over on error or timeout, with an explicit override; no automatic task-class routing until the local model's quality is measured
* D28 — ARIA may reconfigure the shared Ollama instance (residency, concurrency, preloading), making that config ARIA-managed state in the umbrella Helm chart (D15) and ARIA a co-owner of shared homelab infrastructure

**Open**

* Which local model is used, and whether a tool-calling-capable one must be pulled onto the GPU node — owned by ARIA-109, which also gates D35's revisit trigger. This story stays implementable ahead of it because host and model are config-driven

issues.description:
Stand the service up empty: it compiles, serves gRPC, connects to Postgres and Qdrant, and can apply migrations. Every schema and API story in this epic builds on it.

**Not this story:** deploying Postgres and Qdrant to k3s — Deployment & Infra owns the operator choice, StatefulSets and volumes. The workspace and `proto/` codegen setup is Platform Foundation's; this story consumes it.

**Acceptance criteria**

* The crate builds inside the `aria` workspace and starts a `tonic` server answering a health/readiness RPC; Postgres URL, Qdrant URL and listen address load at start-up and the process fails fast with a clear message when a required value is missing
* The service's own `.proto` lives in the shared `proto/` directory, generates Rust that compiles, and is wired into the gRPC module tree
* Every RPC that touches user data carries an explicit `user_id`; the propagated identity context is read from gRPC metadata only, never accepted as an LLM-fillable tool argument
* A Postgres connection pool and a `qdrant-client` connection are established at start-up, and a migration harness applies everything in `migrations/`; running it twice is a no-op
* A local dev stack (docker-compose or equivalent) brings up Postgres and Qdrant, with a single documented command that runs the integration tests against it
* A smoke integration test connecting to both stores and applying a baseline (empty) migration passes in CI
* Postgres access uses `sqlx` with compile-time-checked queries, and the migration harness above is `sqlx`'s own

**Decisions**

* D23 — `sqlx` with compile-time-checked queries and its built-in migration harness; every later schema story in this epic must use the same choice
* D19 — recursive CTEs over the `relationship` table are one of the two places an ORM would add friction, which is why `sqlx` won
* D10 — the Knowledge Core is a deployed service owning both stores, not a shared library, so DB credentials stay in one workload

**Open**

* The Confluence directory layout (`services/knowledge-core/`, `migrations/`, `tests/`) is a proposal, not a decision; this story adopts or adjusts it and records what was chosen

* The both-backends-unavailable case produces the decided behaviour as a typed gRPC error within the request timeout — never a hang or an empty success
* Every request records which backend served it, and whether a fallback occurred, as a tracing field consumable by the Observability stack
* Failover triggers on **error or timeout** only; an explicit per-request or config-level override can force the local backend, and a test asserts no code path performs automatic task-class routing

issues.description:
Produce the agreed schema for people and the typed relationships between them, replacing the legacy `relation`/`relation_type` tables and the sharded whiteboard graph store. The modelling approach, key and ownership column are fixed; **the column list is this story's output**.

**Not this story:** writing the migration and the gRPC API (ARIA-59); the delegation flow itself.

**Acceptance criteria**

* A schema proposal (ERD plus draft DDL) covering people and typed relationships is written down, linked from this issue, and agreed before any migration is merged
* Every legacy concept — `relation`, `relation_type`, and `Master`/`Node`/`Source`/`Edge`/`UID` — is mapped into the new schema or recorded as deliberately dropped with a reason
* The proposal states how a person record relates to a Keycloak login, handling person ≠ account explicitly
* The model supports directed, typed relationships including at least one non-symmetric type, and states whether relationship types are a closed enum in code or data rows addable at runtime
* The proposal documents the maximum traversal depth the relational design must serve, and which questions are answered by semantic retrieval instead
* The proposal names which fields exist purely as hooks for later work (e.g. delegation) versus fields with behaviour today
* The proposal builds on the fixed inputs rather than reopening them: typed `person` plus `relationship(from, to, type, attrs JSONB)`, `person.id` as an ARIA UUID with a nullable unique `keycloak_sub`, and `owner_user_id` on every row

**Decisions**

* D19 — typed `person` plus a `relationship(from, to, type, attrs JSONB)` edge table with an enumerated relation type; columns remain this story's output
* D17 — `person.id` is an ARIA UUID, `keycloak_sub` a nullable unique link to a realm account; `sub` (D2) stays the wire identity, `person.id` the graph identity
* D18 — every row carries `owner_user_id` and reads filter on it; the accepted cost is duplicate rows for one real person across owners, deliberately not deduplicated (ARIA-59)
* D4 — some circle members hold realm accounts and some never will, so `person` rows must exist without a Keycloak subject

**Open**

* The column list: the relationship types and whether they are code or data, `person`'s attributes, what belongs in `attrs JSONB` versus a real column, and which fields are later-work hooks. Nothing here is settled until this design is reviewed

Implements `src/retrieval.rs` — step (1) of the per-request flow: when to retrieve, what to ask for, and how to assemble the result into a prompt.

**Not this story:** the Knowledge Core's schema, storage and retrieval API are the Knowledge Core epic's; the conversation-history schema and accessors are ARIA-115. This story owns the invocation.

**Acceptance criteria**

* `src/retrieval.rs` calls the Knowledge Core over gRPC while handling a `Decide` request, behind a small internal interface that can be faked in tests
* Every retrieval call passes an explicit `user_id` from the propagated context — never an implicit "current user", never a value parsed from request text or produced by the model
* Assembly produces the `LlmBackend` payload under a bounded size cap so a large retrieval cannot overflow the context window; the selection/truncation strategy is deterministic and unit-tested against a fixture larger than the cap
* Knowledge Core unavailability or timeout degrades gracefully: `Decide` still answers with no retrieved context, and the degradation is a tracing field rather than a failed request
* A test asserts retrieved content is data only: text inside a retrieved item that looks like an instruction cannot alter the identity context or change which tools are offered
* Retrieval latency and the number of items retrieved are emitted as tracing fields
* Assembly includes the session's conversation history for the propagated `session_id` alongside retrieved material, and both count against the same size cap
* The payload feeds a **streaming** `LlmBackend` call, so assembly must complete before the first chunk is emitted; its latency is measured as part of time-to-first-token

**Decisions**

* D36 — conversation history is part of assembly: the Agent Core owns it per `session_id` and persists it to the Knowledge Core
* D37 — `Decide` is server-streaming, so assembly sits on the critical path to first audio

**Open**

* How retrieved context is formatted into the prompt — verbatim block, structured fields, or summarised
* Whether retrieval runs once per `Decide` request or can re-run mid tool-calling loop after new information arrives
* What query the Agent Core sends (raw user text vs. a derived query) and how many items it requests

Implement the agreed design as real tables and the first user-facing gRPC surface of the Knowledge Core (`grpc/people.rs`).

**Not this story:** JWT validation and the context-verification helper — the Identity epic owns `aria-identity`. Preferences follow separately.

**Acceptance criteria**

* A migration creates the people and relationship tables from the agreed design; it applies cleanly to an empty database, is a no-op on re-run, and has a working rollback path or a documented reason it cannot have one
* `grpc/people.rs` exposes create, read, update, delete and list for people, and create/list/delete for relationships, with an explicit `user_id` on every call
* The identity context is taken from propagated gRPC metadata via `aria-identity` and never from a request body field; a test asserts a request whose body claims a different subject than the metadata context is rejected
* Relationship reads return both directions for symmetric types and only the correct direction for non-symmetric types, proven by tests for each
* Referential integrity is enforced: a relationship to a non-existent person, or deleting a person that still has relationships, produces a defined, tested outcome rather than a constraint error leaking as an opaque internal gRPC status
* Integration tests run against the local dev Postgres and cover the full lifecycle plus at least two invalid-input rejections
* Every read filters on `owner_user_id`: a test proves a traversal for user A never returns a person or relationship owned by user B, and that a user can traverse an edge they own even when it points at a person another user also knows

**Decisions**

* D18 — per-fact ownership: `owner_user_id` on every row and reads filtered on it, so traversal works inside your own graph while facts another circle member contributed stay invisible

**Open**

* Cross-owner person deduplication. D18 accepts that the same real person may exist as several rows under different owners and sets no policy; until one exists this story stores the duplicates rather than merging them, and no read crosses an owner boundary

The shared crate every deployed service — Gateway, Speech, Agent Core, MCP Registry, Knowledge Core —  
calls at startup: a `tracing-subscriber` registry with a `tracing-opentelemetry` layer over an
`opentelemetry-otlp` exporter, uniform resource attributes, flush on shutdown. Subscriber and  
exporter wiring only; `aria-identity` is a library crate, not a deployed service, and is not a target.

**Not this story:** per-service spans and attributes belong to each service's own epic; the Cargo  
workspace is Platform Foundation.

**Acceptance criteria**

* One documented init call configures subscriber and exporter; a service that adds the crate and calls it emits a span to a local OTLP receiver, with no other code changes
* OTLP endpoint, protocol and auth headers read from configuration at runtime; retargeting to a different OTLP backend needs no code change and no recompile
* No AppSignal-specific crate in the dependency tree and no AppSignal-specific identifier outside test fixtures — asserted by an automated check, not code review
* `service.name`, `service.version` and `deployment.environment` on every exported span, asserted on a captured span
* With telemetry disabled by config the service starts, serves traffic, and makes zero OTLP connection attempts
* Exporter failure (endpoint unreachable, TLS error, collector down) never panics and never blocks the request path — tested against a dead endpoint, request still completing within normal latency
* Init wires **all three signals** — traces, logs, metrics — over OTLP to the same collector; logs bridged from `tracing` at reduced level, allow-listed fields only (the allow-list is ARIA-66's output)
* Vendor-neutrality, config-driven endpoint and disable-by-config hold for the log and metric pipelines too; the automated checks cover all three signals

**Decisions**

* D41 — all three signals leave via the collector, so this crate wires logs and metrics as well as traces; accepted cost is the less mature Rust logs bridge

**Open**

issues.description:
Implements `src/tools.rs` — steps (2) and (3) of the per-request flow, plus the hard security property on the loop: nothing the model emits can alter who the caller is.

**Not this story:** MCP server connections, tool aggregation, dynamic registration and consent enforcement are the MCP Registry's — the Agent Core is a client. Conversational prompt-and-retry is ARIA-118.

**Acceptance criteria**

* `src/tools.rs` fetches the current toolset from the MCP Registry per request and passes it to `LlmBackend` in the neutral schema; a test proves a newly exposed tool becomes callable with no Agent Core code change
* On a model tool call the Agent Core asks the Registry to execute it, feeds the result back and repeats until a final answer; a test drives at least a two-tool-call conversation to completion
* **Prompt-injection property:** a test proves a model-emitted `user_id` (or role/identity) argument cannot override the propagated context — it is rejected or stripped, and the Registry call carries only the infrastructure-injected identity
* A second injection test uses a user message instructing the model to act as a different person, and asserts the executed Registry call still carries the original `user_id`
* Tool failures and Registry-side denials, including consent refusals, go back to the model as tool results so it can respond, not aborting the request or being retried blindly
* The loop is bounded; hitting the bound produces a defined response to the caller instead of a hang, and the event is traced
* MCP Registry unavailability has defined behaviour — answer without tools, or a typed error — not an unhandled failure
* **No MCP SDK dependency**; all tool traffic is gRPC to the Registry, with tool schemas as JSON Schema in the proto contract
* The toolset the model sees is **server-filtered, not tool-filtered**, so it may legitimately hold ungranted tools; the loop must not filter, hide or pre-reject them on grant state
* A `consent required` result is a **distinct outcome** — not a tool failure, not an ordinary tool result
* A tool call is **never auto-retried**; only read-only calls such as fetching the toolset retry with backoff

**Decisions**

* D9 — enforcement identity comes only from the Gateway's signed context; the **MCP Registry**, not the Agent Core, injects contextual identity into a reserved `_aria_user_id` argument, stripped from the model's schemas and overwritten if present
* D38 — no MCP client SDK; a single path to MCP servers is what makes the consent-enforcement claim true
* D46 — `ListTools` filters by server, so the model may be offered an ungranted tool; that is intended, since it is how the consent prompt fires
* D42 — `consent required` is not a failure; prompt-and-retry is ARIA-118, this story only keeps it distinguishable
* D39 — read-only calls retry with backoff; anything that can execute a tool never does

**Open**

* The iteration bound and any per-request tool-call limit — no decision fixes the numbers
* Whether the toolset is fetched fresh per request or cached with invalidation, given the "available immediately" requirement

issues.description:
The structured half of preferences: an attribute store attached to a person, plus a seam for the semantic half.

**Not this story:** the free-text half of preferences is authoritative in Qdrant and belongs to ARIA-76.

**Acceptance criteria**

* A migration adds preference/attribute storage attached to a person such that a new kind of preference requires no schema change; key namespacing and value typing are documented in the migration
* gRPC set, get, list and delete for an explicit `user_id`; set is an upsert safe to call repeatedly with the same value, yielding exactly one row
* Every attribute row carries an `owner_user_id` — the user the preference was learned from — and every read filters on it; a test asserts one circle member's preferences are not returned to another
* Each attribute row records its provenance — which caller wrote it and when — so the write-permission model can act on it later without a schema change
* Whether a preference write also produces or updates an embedded copy is driven by the embed-vs-structured decision; the code calls through an interface rather than inlining the answer, and a test covers whichever behaviour that decision fixes
* Listing preferences for a person with none returns an empty result rather than an error; reading an unknown key returns a distinguishable "not set", not a default value
* Integration tests cover set, overwrite, list, delete, and deletion of the owning person removing or orphaning attributes per the documented rule
* That provenance is the D21 `source`; the Knowledge Core rejects a write from a service modifying a row it did not author or touching an undeclared area — enforced here, not only at the MCP Registry; both rejection paths tested

**Decisions**

* D16 — preferences are partitioned by kind: this story owns the typed/Postgres half, so there is no dual-write and no "which store wins" question; the rule classifying a given preference is ARIA-43's output
* D18 — per-fact ownership: every preference row carries `owner_user_id` and reads filter on it, so facts learned from one circle member are not disclosed to another. `owner_user_id` and D21's `source` are different columns — which _user_ the fact came from, versus which _service_ wrote the row
* D21 — every row carries a `source`; a server may only modify rows it authored, and its KC areas are declared at registration
* D22 — the Knowledge Core validates writes itself from the caller's client-credentials identity, independently of the Registry's gate. Accepted cost: the rule lives in two places and must not drift

issues.description:
The feedback path out of the orchestrator: detect an unrecognized request and write it back to the Knowledge Core.

**Not this story:** the Knowledge Core owns the storage schema and the write API. This story owns detecting the condition and making the call.

**Acceptance criteria**

* On an unrecognized `Decide` request the Agent Core writes a record holding at least the request text, the `user_id` from the propagated context, a timestamp, and which LLM backend served it
* The write is decoupled from the user's answer: a Knowledge Core write failure or timeout never turns a successful response into an error, and the failure is traced
* The classification rule lives in exactly one place, is documented in code, and is unit-tested against fixtures of both kinds — including at least one case that must NOT be logged (a request answered successfully via a tool call)
* The logged `user_id` comes from the propagated context only, never from request text or model output
* No credential, token or raw JWT is in the record; a test asserts the payload contains only the fields listed above
* Repeated identical unknowns behave per an explicitly documented rule — deduplicated or written each time — rather than being left as accidental behaviour; **which** of the two is the open item below
* The classifier is purely structural: unrecognized ⇔ **no successful tool call was made AND retrieval returned nothing above the relevance threshold**; a test asserts it consumes no model-reported confidence or self-assessment signal
* Tool-loop iteration-bound exhaustion (ARIA-61) is logged **separately and always**, independent of that classification; a test covers a bound-exhaustion case logged as such and not as an unrecognized request

**Decisions**

* D40 — "unrecognized" is structural, and every tool-loop bound exhaustion is logged regardless; deliberately not model self-reported confidence, which is unreliable and would differ between the hosted and Ollama backends (D35)
* D55 — the record holds the **raw utterance**, bounded by a 90-day window rather than by redaction, so the first criterion above stands as written

**Open**

* Whether unknowns are deduplicated, and whether they are written through the same Knowledge Core API used for retrieval or a dedicated one

issues.description:
A cache of **materialised occurrences** plus accessors — not a calendar schema. An external calendar is authoritative, so ARIA never expands recurrence, resolves a recurring-series exception, performs timezone arithmetic or models attendee state.

**Not this story:** talking to the external calendar provider. Fetching occurrences and user-initiated calendar writes go through the calendar MCP server, ARIA-120; create/update/delete here exist only to keep the cache in step with the authoritative calendar.

**Acceptance criteria**

* A migration creates calendar storage owned by an explicit `user_id`, where an entry carries at minimum a start and end instant, a title and a free-text body
* gRPC create, update, delete and query; the range query's inclusive/exclusive boundary semantics are documented and covered by a test including an entry starting exactly at the range end
* Every method is scoped by explicit `user_id`, with a test proving one user's range query never returns another's entries
* Index coverage for the range query is proven against a seeded dataset large enough that a sequential scan would show up
* Integration tests cover overlapping entries, zero-length and multi-day entries, an empty range, and delete
* The store holds materialised occurrences only; a review of the migration confirms no field would require ARIA to expand a recurrence, resolve a series exception, do timezone arithmetic or model attendee state

**Decisions**

* D20 — the calendar is a mirror with a read-through cache; the external calendar (Google/CalDAV) is the source of truth and writes go through a calendar MCP server, which no story created before ARIA-120

**Open**

* Cache invalidation and refresh cadence — how often the mirror re-reads the external calendar, and what triggers a refresh — is left open by D20 and not settled here

**Removed 2026-08-12 (D20), recorded rather than silently dropped:** the criterion requiring instants in one documented representation (UTC) with the originating timezone alongside, plus a DST round-trip test. Occurrences arrive already materialised as absolute instants, so that arithmetic sits upstream of ARIA. The previously open questions on recurring events and attendees leave this story's scope for the same reason.

issues.description:
A span and attribute convention plus an allow-list encoded as data in `aria-observability` and  
applied before export, so recording conversation or voice content is hard by construction rather than  
forbidden by documentation. The collector is the other enforcement point, but enforcement there alone is  
a single point of failure.

**Not this story:** adding spans to any service (each service's own epic); collector-side scrubbing  
rules are ARIA-74 — this is the in-process half.

**Acceptance criteria**

* A written convention fixes span-name format for gRPC server and client spans, the required resource and span attributes, and each one's permitted value shape (enum, bounded identifier, numeric, duration) — no free-text attribute values anywhere
* The forbidden data classes are enumerated by name — transcribed speech; LLM prompts and completions; retrieved knowledge-base content; MCP tool-call arguments and results; user identifiers — each mapped to the service and code path where it originates
* The allow-list ships as data inside `aria-observability` and applies to every span before export; document and allow-list cannot drift, being generated from or tested against the same source
* A test records a non-allow-listed attribute key and asserts it is absent from the exported span — the span still exports, the attribute does not
* A test records an allow-listed key whose value violates its permitted shape (free text in a bounded enum field) and asserts the value is dropped or replaced, not exported verbatim
* The convention is published where the other epics read it and linked from each service epic
* **One list, not two:** the same allow-list and value shapes govern log record fields as well as span attributes, with the equivalent drop test for a non-allow-listed log field

**Decisions**

* D41 — logs export through the same collector carrying allow-listed fields only, so this list covers log fields too; it settles nothing about whether user identity may appear

**Open**

* Whether user identity appears in telemetry at all — a pseudonymous stable ID surviving across traces, a per-trace ephemeral ID, or omitted entirely. One household means a stable ID is close to a name; the allow-list must not ship a silent choice

* `grpc/registry.rs` exposes CRUD for servers plus a single call that replaces a server's declared tool set atomically, the diff reflected in one transaction
* The server record carries the approval state as data the Registry can read; this story stores and exposes it and explicitly does not implement the PR-based approval process
* Registry and tool rows are infrastructure-level, not user-scoped: these RPCs take no `user_id`, and that asymmetry is documented in the proto comments
* Integration tests cover register, refresh with added and removed tools, delete-with-tools behaviour, and rejection of a duplicate tool name on the same server

A workspace crate wrapping the SDK chosen by ARIA-65: open a session to a server URL, list its tools, call a tool, close. A plain MCP client and nothing more — no consent logic, no user context, no ARIA control-plane concepts leak into it.

**Not this story:** enforcement, consent and registration stay in the MCP Registry's control plane; the protocol itself is never forked.

* Calling a tool forwards arguments verbatim and distinguishes, as separate typed Rust errors, at minimum: transport failure, protocol/JSON-RPC error, tool-not-found, and a tool-level error result

* Connection-failure and reconnect policy — retry/backoff, circuit breaking, and how a persistently unreachable server is represented to the caller. Undecided, and to be settled jointly with the registration story (ARIA-75) so the Registry and the crate agree on who owns retries

issues.description:
The per-tool grant table and its read/write accessors. `granted_by` is present from day one as a delegation hook.

**Not this story:** enforcing the gate at tool-call time — MCP Registry epic. The Keycloak client-per-MCP-server consent layer and its account-console revocation — Identity epic. The delegation flow itself: `granted_by` is a schema hook here and nothing more.

**Acceptance criteria**

* A migration creates `consent_grants` keyed on (user, tool) with `granted_by` present from day one; for every grant created today `granted_by` equals the granting user, and the column's purpose as a delegation hook is documented in the migration
* Revocation is explicit state, not a delete: a revoked grant stays distinguishable from one that never existed, and re-granting after revocation is supported and tested
* A single index-backed accessor answers "does user X currently hold a grant for tool Y" for the Registry's hot path, with a test proving a revoked or expired-by-policy grant answers no
* Grants are per tool, not per server: a test proves a grant for one tool does not imply a grant for a sibling tool on the same server
* Additional accessors list all grants for a user (for a future account-facing view) and revoke a grant, both taking an explicit `user_id`
* Integration tests cover grant, revoke, re-grant, query for an unknown tool, query for a user with no grants, and a grant referencing a tool whose server was deleted

* D42 — grants are written conversationally: the Registry returns `consent required`, the Agent Core asks, and on approval the grant is written here and the original call retried automatically within a bounded timeout. Keycloak's account console stays the review and revocation surface

* Whether grants expire or are open-ended
* Whether revoking an `aria:mcp:<server-slug>:<tool>` scope in Keycloak cascades to the matching row here, or the two layers are independent — needs agreement with the Identity and MCP Registry epics

issues.description:
AppSignal's **self-hosted** collector (not their hosted one) in the `aria` namespace, as the only path telemetry takes out of the cluster. Not routing but a privacy boundary: telemetry stays local until scrubbed, and that only holds if no service can export past it.

**Not this story:** the collector's Kubernetes **manifest** and the workload mechanics around it — packaging, secret management, network policy — belong to Infra's umbrella Helm chart (D15, D33). The scrubbing **rules** are ARIA-74; this story wires that pipeline in, it does not define it.

**Acceptance criteria**

* Runs in the `aria` namespace at a stable in-cluster OTLP endpoint, all five services pointed at it through the `aria-observability` config surface; a smoke test from a service pod lands a visible span
* Egress policy blocks any service pod reaching an external telemetry endpoint directly; a negative test from a pod attempting a direct outbound OTLP/HTTPS connection to a non-collector destination fails
* AppSignal credentials come from a Kubernetes Secret — never the image, a ConfigMap or a committed file; a check asserts no credential-shaped string in version-controlled manifests
* Collector restart or unavailability degrades telemetry only: services keep serving across a deliberate outage
* The collector config is version-controlled, and a documented rollback swaps the export destination for a local OTLP sink with no service code change and no image redeploy
* Sized and configured for **all three signals** on one instance, the egress negative test covering log and metric endpoints as well as traces
* A check asserts the deployed config is the version-controlled one

**Decisions**

* D41 — logs and metrics route through this same collector, so sizing and the egress test assume all three signals
* D33 — the Observability _epic_ owns the collector's config and its scrubbing pipeline while Infra owns the manifest. Within the epic, this story owns the collector and its config surface; ARIA-74 owns the scrubbing rules that run inside it
* D15 — one umbrella Helm chart for the namespace, Infra-owned, is what forces that split

**Open**

* Telemetry retention: how long anything is kept at the collector, and whether anything is persisted in-cluster at all versus forwarded only
* Alerting rules on this data are entirely undecided; none is delivered here
* The fallback OTLP target if AppSignal's beta Rust support disappoints — the rollback _mechanism_ is a criterion above, the destination it points at is not chosen

issues.description:
Collector processor configuration that redacts or drops by rule, treating anything not explicitly  
permitted as suspect — the last point at which telemetry is still local. The in-process allow-list  
(ARIA-66) sits in the binaries that produce the content and can be bypassed by a service  
constructing spans directly.

**Not this story:** the end-to-end leak test through real services is ARIA-77; this story tests the  
collector config in isolation.

**Acceptance criteria**

* The pipeline drops any span attribute whose key is not on the shared allow-list, and any log record body that is not a bounded, structured message — default-deny, so an attribute added tomorrow does not export by default
* Each of the five leak paths has an explicit rule and a test — transcribed speech (`aria-speech`), LLM prompts and completions (`aria-agent-core`), retrieved knowledge-base content (`aria-knowledge-core`), MCP tool-call arguments and results (`aria-mcp-registry`), user identifiers (all services, from the Gateway) — a payload carrying a marked string in that shape goes in, and no occurrence of it comes out
* Redaction covers span names, span attributes, span events, resource attributes and log bodies — not attributes alone, since a span _name_ built from user input leaks just as well
* Redaction and drop actions increment a visible counter, so a rule that starts matching everything, or nothing, is detectable
* The collector config is version-controlled and its tests run against the same file that is deployed — no separate fixture that can drift
* A deliberately misconfigured pipeline (one rule removed) fails its test suite, proving the tests constrain the config rather than passing vacuously
* Default-deny rules and their tests cover the **log and metric pipelines** as well as traces, including metric names and attributes, so no signal type has a weaker rule set

**Decisions**

* D41 — logs and metrics do not bypass this collector; there is no second egress path and therefore no second enforcement point to build

**Open**

* Whether a scrubbing failure fails closed (drop the payload) or open (export with a warning). Closed protects privacy and loses observability exactly when something is going wrong; open does the reverse

issues.description:
The admin gRPC API and its persistence — the "connect a new system without much intervention" requirement. Standard MCP does not provide dynamic runtime registration, so it lives in the Registry's control plane rather than in a forked protocol.

**Not this story:** the `mcp_tools` table schema belongs to the Knowledge Core epic and is written through its API; deploying MCP servers as k8s workloads belongs to Deployment & Infra.

**Acceptance criteria**

* `RegisterServer` accepts an in-cluster DNS name or a LAN HTTP URL, opens a streamable-HTTP MCP session through the `mcp-client` crate, and discovers the server's tool list as part of registration
* A registration whose `initialize` handshake or tool discovery fails is rejected with a descriptive error and persists nothing — no half-registered server records
* On success the server record (id, URL, associated Keycloak client reference, registered-at) and the discovered tool inventory persist through the Knowledge Core, and both rehydrate on restart without re-registration
* `DeregisterServer` closes the session and marks the record removed; afterwards the server's tools are absent from `ListTools` and a `CallTool` against them is rejected without a network call
* Re-registering an already-known URL refreshes the existing record's inventory instead of creating a duplicate
* Accepted and rejected registrations are both `tracing`-instrumented with the server identity, rejections with the reason
* The record carries the stable slug and, for in-cluster servers, the approved image digest; the per-tool Keycloak scopes a registration needs are provisioned by calling `aria-kc-broker` (ARIA-110), and a test asserts this service holds no Keycloak admin credential of its own

* D44 — approval is read from `approved-servers.yaml` in git, rendered into the Helm chart; merging the PR that adds an entry is the approval
* D45 — approval is matched on the container image digest, with a stable slug as the Registry's key, so a rebuild requires re-approval. **Recorded weakness:** remote LAN servers have no digest and fall back to URL plus a pinned certificate — a genuinely weaker gate, documented as such rather than presented as equivalent
* D8 — the per-tool scopes `aria:mcp:<server>:<tool>` a registration implies are provisioned via `aria-kc-broker`, never by this service holding a Keycloak admin credential

**Open**

* Tool-list drift: whether the persisted inventory refreshes on a schedule, on every `ListTools`, or only on re-registration; and what happens to existing per-tool grants when a tool's input schema changes or the tool disappears. Direct consent-enforcement consequences
* How a persistently unreachable registered server is represented — degraded status, or auto-deregistered. Coupled to ARIA-69's reconnect-policy question

issues.description:
The RAG half of the Knowledge Core: collection provisioning in `db/qdrant.rs` and the embed/retrieve API over it. Qdrant holds primary data, not a rebuildable index.

**Not this story:** deciding when to retrieve and how to assemble a prompt — the Agent Core owns the request path, this story owns the API it calls. Deploying Qdrant is Deployment & Infra.

**Acceptance criteria**

* `db/qdrant.rs` ensures the collection(s) exist at start-up using the vector dimension and distance metric fixed by the embedding-model decision; running against an already-provisioned collection is a no-op and never destroys data
* Every point payload carries the owning `user_id` and the retrieval RPC applies that filter server-side; a test proves a query for user A cannot return a point owned by user B
* `grpc/memory.rs` exposes a write path (store a fact/preference/conversation excerpt, embedded through the embedder abstraction) and a retrieval path (top-k search with metadata filters and a score threshold), results carrying enough payload to trace back to the Postgres row when the item is dual-stored
* Deleting or updating the structured source of a dual-stored item propagates to its vector per the embed-vs-structured consistency rule; tested in both directions
* Vectors record which embedding model/version produced them, so a model change is a re-embedding migration rather than silent quality drift
* Integration tests against the local dev Qdrant: store then retrieve returns the item above threshold, an unrelated query does not, k and threshold are honoured, and a query against an empty collection returns empty rather than erroring
* Every point payload also carries the D21 `source`; the Knowledge Core itself rejects a write from a service modifying a vector it did not author or touching an undeclared area; both rejection paths tested
* No operation treats the collection as re-derivable: no rebuild-from-Postgres path, and destructive collection operations are not offered as a recovery mechanism

**Decisions**

* D16 — Qdrant is authoritative for free-text preferences (typed ones are Postgres, ARIA-62), so **Qdrant holds primary data**: provisioning, deletes and re-embedding are written on that basis and backup/restore (ARIA-96) treats it as a source of truth. Classification is ARIA-43's output
* D21 — every row, vectors included, carries a `source`; a server may only modify what it authored, with KC areas declared at registration
* D22 — the Knowledge Core enforces that itself from the caller's client-credentials identity, so network access is not authority to write. Accepted cost: the rule lives in two places and must not drift

**Open**

* Which embedder and which vector dimension — ARIA-52's output, and the input `db/qdrant.rs` cannot provision a collection without
* The retrieval API signature needs review with Agent Core before it is treated as stable

issues.description:
Gate **(1)** of the two-gate model, and it is about _code_, not users: a check that runs inside `RegisterServer` before anything is persisted or connected.

**Not this story:** consent — per-user, ongoing and revocable — is the two consent-gate stories (ARIA-88, ARIA-90). Approval is one-time and admin-level.

**Acceptance criteria**

* `RegisterServer` for a server identity absent from the approved-servers source is rejected with a permission error; no session is opened and nothing is persisted
* The approved-servers source is admin-controlled and PR-based: a test asserts there is no Registry gRPC method and no runtime code path that can add or modify an approval
* A registration originating from the Self-Extension flow passes through exactly the same gate — a test covers a self-generated server being refused while unapproved
* Approval is matched on a stable server identity rather than a mutable display name; a request presenting an approved identity with a mismatching endpoint/identity attribute is refused
* Both accepted and refused registrations record the identity checked and the approval decision, so an unapproved registration attempt is visible after the fact
* A rebuilt image is refused: a registration presenting a known slug with an image digest absent from `approved-servers.yaml` is rejected exactly like an unknown server, covered by a test

**Decisions**

* D44 — the approved-servers source is `approved-servers.yaml` in the repository, rendered into the Helm chart and read as deployed config; merging the PR **is** the approval, so nothing ARIA runs can grant itself approval
* D45 — the stable identity is the container image digest, with a slug as the Registry's key. **Recorded weakness:** remote LAN servers have no digest and fall back to URL plus a pinned certificate — a genuinely weaker gate, to be documented as such

**Links:** [Decision Log — observability & consent](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/decisions/0007-observability-consent.md) · [MCP Registry](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/services/mcp-registry.md) · [Self-Extension](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/services/self-extension.md)

issues.description:
**Context**

CLAUDE.md §4: "ARIA runs on **Jann's existing k3s cluster** at home, in its own `aria` namespace — not a new cluster, not a cloud VPS."

CLAUDE.md does _not_ record the cluster's node count, which StorageClass is available, which GPU runtime makes Ollama work on the GPU node, or whether a container registry already exists in the homelab. Every other story in this epic sizes itself off those facts, so establish and write them down first.

This is a read-only investigation of the _existing_ cluster plus a durable written record. No workloads are deployed here.

**Acceptance criteria**

* A cluster inventory is written down: node count, k3s version, per-node labels and taints, and which node carries the GPU.
* Every StorageClass is listed with its provisioner, default flag, reclaim policy and whether it supports volume expansion; the one ARIA's PVCs will use is named, or the gap is flagged as a decision.
* The GPU node's existing runtime config is documented in enough detail to copy into a manifest: device plugin/runtime in use (NVIDIA device plugin or ROCm, "whichever is set up" per §4), the resource name a pod requests, and any taint a pod must tolerate — derived from how Ollama already runs there.
* It is established whether a container registry is already reachable from the cluster (in-cluster, LAN or hosted) and whether nodes would need an imagePullSecret for it.
* The reachable in-cluster/LAN endpoints (DNS name/URL + port) of the _existing_ Keycloak and Ollama are recorded, without changing either of them.
* Findings live in a durable location (repo doc or Confluence) that the other stories in this epic can reference by link.

**Open / needs decision:**

* Which StorageClass ARIA uses, and whether its provisioner is adequate for the stateful datastores.
* Whether a container registry exists or one has to be chosen/stood up — CLAUDE.md names no registry.

**Out of scope**

* Deploying or reconfiguring Keycloak and Ollama. CLAUDE.md §6: "Not standing up new infrastructure that duplicates what's already running (Keycloak, Ollama, Kubernetes) — extend the existing homelab instead."
* The GPU memory budget and STT/TTS model selection (Speech epic).

comments.author: FPG Schiba
comments.body:
**Partial progress 2026-08-19: the GPU-runtime criterion is answered. The rest of the baseline is not.**

While debugging an Ollama outage, the GPU node's runtime config was established — one of this story's acceptance criteria ("the GPU node's existing runtime config is documented in enough detail to copy into a manifest ... derived from how Ollama already runs there").

**Finding: it is not a Kubernetes GPU runtime at all.** Ollama runs in **LXC container CT 200** on Proxmox host `prox2`, with the GPU exposed by bind-mounted device nodes plus `lxc.cgroup2.devices.allow` rules — not via an NVIDIA device plugin, and not vfio passthrough to a VM. GPU: **RTX 2070, 8 GB**, driver 580.173.02 (`.run` installer), CUDA 13.0.

**This matters for** `04-deployment.md`'s assumption. That section says `aria-speech` is "pinned (nodeSelector/toleration) to the GPU node, reusing whatever GPU runtime config already makes Ollama work there." If the GPU currently reaches Ollama through an LXC bind mount rather than through Kubernetes, **there may be no k8s-visible GPU resource to request at all** — no `nvidia.com/gpu` to put in a pod spec. Whether the k3s cluster is the same machine, and whether an NVIDIA device plugin exists on it, is still unknown and remains this story's job.

**An outage worth recording as a baseline finding in its own right.**

After a host power-cycle, Ollama ran **100% on CPU while appearing entirely healthy** — API responsive, models listed, generation \~50x too slow. Root cause: the NVIDIA driver creates `/dev/nvidia*` lazily on first use, so at container start the nodes did not exist on the host. With `lxc.mount.entry: ... bind,optional,create=file`, LXC created **empty regular files** instead of device nodes and suppressed the error:

```
----------  1 root root        0  /dev/nvidia0      <- regular file, not a device
crw-rw-rw-  1 root root 195, 255  /dev/nvidiactl    <- the one that happened to exist in time
```

The `cgroup2` allow rules were correct throughout (195:0, 195:255, 510:0/1, 235:1/2 all matched the host majors) — an earlier device-major-renumbering theory was **wrong**. The cause was purely **ordering**.

Fixed with a systemd unit ordered `Before=pve-guests.service` running `nvidia-modprobe -c 0 -u` plus `nvidia-persistenced`. Persistence mode now On. **The reboot test has not yet been performed**, so this is fixed-but-unverified.

**Three consequences for the deployment design:**

1. **A silent CPU fallback is worse than a crash.** A pod that starts, passes its health check and runs 50x too slow pages nobody. `aria-speech` should assert GPU availability at startup and refuse readiness without it (affects ARIA-42, ARIA-93).
2. **The alerting gap is now concrete.** It was deferred on the grounds that there is "nothing to alert on until services run" — this is a counter-example that already happened: a silent capability loss with no signal.
3. **Verification must not use** `nvidia-smi` — running it _creates_ the device nodes it is meant to check for. The only valid test is `ls -l /dev/nvidia*` after a reboot, before touching anything NVIDIA.

**Still outstanding for this story:** node count (D6 depends on it), StorageClasses, whether the CNI actually enforces NetworkPolicy (ARIA-117 — k3s ships flannel, which does not), whether a container registry exists, and the in-cluster endpoints of Keycloak and Ollama. **D6's two triggers remain unchecked.** Script ready at `scripts/aria-cluster-baseline.sh`; write-up at `docs/spikes/ARIA-27-gpu-baseline.md`.

comments.author: FPG Schiba
comments.body:
**Four findings, 2026-08-19 — three contradict CLAUDE.md §4, and one has fired a decision's revisit trigger.** Discovered while setting up kubectl access, before the full baseline script ran. The remaining criteria (StorageClasses, registry, NetworkPolicy enforcement) are still outstanding.

**1. It is not k3s. It is kubeadm v1.33.0** — containerd 2.0.5, Ubuntu 24.04.1 LTS, `/usr/bin/kubeadm`, `/etc/kubernetes/`. CLAUDE.md §2/§4 and several story descriptions say "k3s" and are wrong. Consequences: there is no `/etc/rancher/k3s/registries.yaml`; the API server runs as an inspectable static pod; and **kubeadm ships no CNI**, so one was chosen deliberately — which matters for finding 4.

**2. 🔴 TWO NODES — D6's first revisit trigger has FIRED.**

```
kube-control     control-plane   192.168.1.20   v1.33.0
kube-worker-01   <none>          192.168.1.21   v1.33.0
```

D6 kept internal gRPC plaintext and said so conditionally: _"if the cluster turns out to be multi-node, voice audio crosses the LAN in plaintext between nodes and this decision must be revisited rather than inherited."_ It is multi-node. **D6 must be reopened** — superseded by a new entry, not edited. In scope: Gateway↔Speech audio and every inter-service gRPC call that could be scheduled across the two nodes. Options: mTLS, a service mesh, pinning all ARIA workloads to one node, or accepting the risk explicitly with reasoning recorded. Affects ARIA-14, ARIA-42, ARIA-91, ARIA-117.

**3. 🔴 The GPU is NOT in the cluster.** Neither node is 192.168.1.15. The RTX 2070 is on Proxmox host `prox2`, reached by Ollama in LXC CT 200 through bind-mounted device nodes — not through Kubernetes. §4 says _"Speech is pinned (nodeSelector/toleration) to the GPU node"_; **there is no GPU node in this cluster**, so that is not achievable as written. Every option is real work no story covers: join the GPU host as a node (needs passthrough to whatever runs kubelet, plus a device plugin); expose the GPU to an existing node (same problem elsewhere); run `aria-speech` outside Kubernetes (breaks D15's single-umbrella-chart convention); or use hosted STT/TTS (contradicts §4's local-by-default posture).

**This is a bigger rework than D6** — D6 changes how services talk, this changes where one of them can run. **Do not size ARIA-93 or ARIA-46 until it is decided.**

**4. Keycloak's TLS chain is broken, and ARIA inherits the problem.** The cluster's OIDC authentication has never worked. API server logs, every 10 seconds:

```
oidc authenticator: initializing plugin: Get ".../.well-known/openid-configuration":
  tls: failed to verify certificate: x509: certificate signed by unknown authority
-> [invalid bearer token, oidc: authenticator not initialized]
```

The config is correct — issuer, `--oidc-client-id=kubernetes`, `preferred_username`, `groups`, and `--oidc-ca-file` are all live on the running process, and the CA file exists. The failure is the **chain**: `openssl s_client` returns `Verify return code: 21 (unable to verify the first certificate)` — Keycloak serves a leaf **without its intermediate**.

**Why this is ARIA's problem too:** ARIA-20 has `aria-identity` fetch OIDC discovery and JWKS from this same Keycloak over TLS, and every service validates tokens against it. It will fail identically. **Nothing in the backlog distributes that CA to ARIA's pods** — ARIA-81 bootstraps secrets, ARIA-20 assumes discovery works. Per D50, that failure must be loud rather than an unexplained 401, which is exactly the silent degradation the API server is exhibiting now.

Right fix is at the source: make Keycloak serve its full chain, repairing every client at once. Patching `keycloak-ca.crt` fixes Kubernetes only and leaves the same trap for ARIA.

**Still outstanding on this story:** StorageClasses; **whether the CNI enforces NetworkPolicy** (ARIA-117 — D6's _second_ trigger, and since kubeadm required a deliberate CNI choice this may well be enforced, unlike k3s+flannel — prove it, don't infer it); container registry; in-cluster vs LAN endpoints for Keycloak and Ollama, both of which appear to be outside the cluster.

Full write-up: `docs/spikes/ARIA-79-cluster-findings-2026-08-19.md`. A contradiction banner has been added to `docs/04-deployment.md` so nobody builds on the three wrong statements.

comments.body:
**Correction to finding 4 in the previous comment.** I said Keycloak was serving a leaf without its intermediate. **That was wrong.** `Verify return code: 21` is consistent with two different causes and I picked the wrong one before checking the certificates. Correcting rather than quietly editing.

**Actual root cause: the API server was told to trust the wrong CA.**

```
Keycloak leaf   subject = O = FPGArmy, CN = keycloak.fpg
                issuer  = C = CH, ST = Local, L = Home, O = FPG, CN = fpg-ca

keycloak-ca.crt subject = CN = My Internal CA      <-- a DIFFERENT CA
                issuer  = CN = My Internal CA      (self-signed)
                dates   = 2025-05-01 .. 2035-04-29
                contains exactly 1 certificate
```

`My Internal CA` is not `fpg-ca`. **There is no intermediate and no chain problem** — Keycloak's certificate is issued directly by the homelab root. `/etc/kubernetes/pki/keycloak-ca.crt` simply holds the wrong certificate, apparently a leftover from May 2025.

**Homelab fix:** replace that file with the real `fpg-ca` root. The API server retries plugin initialisation every 10 seconds, so it should recover without a restart. That is not ARIA work.

**What this changes for ARIA — the gap gets smaller and more concrete.** Because Keycloak's certificate is issued **directly by the root**, distributing trust to ARIA's pods is the simplest possible case: one self-signed root certificate, no chain assembly, no ordering concerns. `fpg-ca` is the homelab's own root and presumably signs every internal service, so solving it once covers everything ARIA talks to internally.

The open item is therefore narrow and clearly ownable: **get** `fpg-ca` into ARIA's pods' trust store — a ConfigMap mounted by the umbrella chart (D15), baked into the base image, or a cluster-wide trust bundle. `aria-identity` (ARIA-20) fetches OIDC discovery and JWKS over that TLS connection and will fail exactly as the API server did without it. **Nothing in the backlog does this yet.**

Per D50, that failure must be loud rather than a silent 401 — which is precisely the silent-degradation shape the API server has been exhibiting.

Findings 1–3 (kubeadm not k3s; two nodes, D6 trigger fired; GPU outside the cluster) are unchanged.

comments.body:
**Closing 2026-08-19.** Every acceptance criterion is met. Evidence in `docs/spikes/ARIA-79-cluster-findings-2026-08-19.md` and `aria-cluster-baseline.txt`.

| Criterion | Outcome |
| --- | --- |
| Cluster inventory: node count, version, labels, taints, which node carries the GPU | **kubeadm v1.33.0**, containerd 2.0.5, Ubuntu 24.04. `kube-control` 192.168.1.20 (tainted `NoSchedule`, 4 vCPU / 3.8 GiB), `kube-worker-01` 192.168.1.21 (schedulable, 4 vCPU / 7.75 GiB). **No node carries a GPU.** Not k3s, as CLAUDE.md claimed |
| Every StorageClass with provisioner, default, reclaim, expansion; name the one ARIA uses | `longhorn` (default) and `longhorn-static`, both `driver.longhorn.io`, `reclaim=Delete`, `expansion=True`. **ARIA uses** `longhorn` — it is the only provisioner present, replicated, and supports expansion, which removes size-it-right-first-time pressure |
| GPU node runtime config, detailed enough to copy into a manifest | **There is none.** No device plugin, no GPU operator, no RuntimeClasses, no node advertising a GPU resource. The GPU is on Proxmox `prox2` reached by Ollama in LXC CT 200 via bind mounts — outside Kubernetes entirely |
| Container registry reachable? imagePullSecret needed? | **Decided** `ghcr.io` (D51, superseded by D52 on corrected reasoning — Harbor is in fact already running). **No** `imagePullSecret` exists anywhere in the cluster today, so that is new work for ARIA-86/ARIA-91 |
| Endpoints of existing Keycloak and Ollama, unchanged | Keycloak is **in-cluster**: `keycloak.keycloak.svc.cluster.local` (80/443), ingress `keycloak.fpg` → 192.168.1.21 via MetalLB/nginx. Issuer `https://keycloak.fpg/realms/master`. Ollama is **outside** the cluster at `http://192.168.1.15:11434` |
| Findings in a durable, linkable location | `docs/spikes/ARIA-79-cluster-findings-2026-08-19.md`, linked from the spikes index and from `04-deployment.md`'s contradiction banner |

**Both "Open / needs decision" items on this story are resolved:** the StorageClass is `longhorn` (above), and the registry is decided (D52).

**Findings that outlived this story and are tracked elsewhere:**

* **D6's first trigger FIRED** — two nodes. D6 must be superseded. Tracked in `docs/open-questions/needs-decision.md`.
* **D6's second trigger did NOT fire** — the CNI is **Antrea**, which enforces NetworkPolicy, and eight policies are already deployed by other charts. Still worth proving empirically with a deny-all test, but the prior is strong. With **cert-manager already running**, mTLS is now a cheap option for the reopening rather than an expensive one.
* **The GPU is not in the cluster** — `04-deployment.md`'s "Speech is pinned to the GPU node" is not achievable as written. Bigger rework than D6. Do not size ARIA-93 or ARIA-46 until decided.
* **Only one schedulable node, 4 vCPU / 7.75 GiB**, already running Harbor, Vault, Longhorn, monitoring, nginx-ingress and MetalLB. ARIA adds six services plus Postgres and Qdrant. **No story sizes this** — raised as an open item.
* **Longhorn's default** `reclaimPolicy: Delete` destroys the volume when a PVC is deleted. Under D16 Qdrant holds primary, non-rebuildable data. `Retain` deserves a deliberate choice in ARIA-87/ARIA-89.
* **Three decisions were argued on infrastructure that already exists** — Harbor, Vault, cert-manager. Full review in `docs/spikes/decision-audit-2026-08-19.md`: D51 superseded, D31 and D41 need re-decisions, six others checked clean.

The `--oidc-*` configuration on the API server was also captured for the ARIA-19 record while investigating a related outage (the cluster's OIDC had never worked — the wrong CA was installed).

issues.description:
Measurement work, not build. Confirm what AppSignal counts as one billable request before assuming  
the free tier (50K requests/month) has headroom: the risk is a definition counting internal spans  
rather than user-visible interactions, multiplying usage by ARIA's five-service fan-out and quietly  
consuming the tier.

**Acceptance criteria**

* A written determination of what AppSignal counts as one billable request for OTLP trace data from a Rust service, from AppSignal's own documentation or a direct answer from them, source cited — not inferred from behaviour alone
* Measured from a real end-to-end interaction through all five services: spans emitted, spans exported after sampling and scrubbing, and units billable under that definition. Measured, not estimated from architecture
* Both a typical short interaction and a heavier one (multi-turn, several MCP tool calls, knowledge retrieval) are measured, since fan-out is not constant per interaction
* An extrapolation to expected monthly volume for the real population — one person plus a small circle — with the interaction-rate assumption stated explicitly, and headroom or shortfall against the 50K/month tier stated as a number
* If headroom is inadequate, the levers (sampling, reducing span cardinality, dropping internal-hop spans, a different OTLP backend) are documented with their trade-offs, none selected — that is a separate decision
* The corresponding entry in `docs/open-questions/` is replaced by the finding and its date, so the question is not re-asked later

**Open**

* Sampling strategy stays undecided and is deliberately not chosen here; this story produces the evidence that decision needs, and head-vs-tail and a rate are downstream of the measurement
* The fallback if AppSignal's beta Rust support proves inadequate — a different OTLP backend, a locally retained store, or no backend at all. Vendor-neutral instrumentation makes it a config change, but no target is chosen

issues.description:
Give the `aria` namespace workload identities, a secret-delivery path, and proof that its pods reach the Keycloak and Ollama already running elsewhere on the cluster/LAN.

**Not this story:** deploying Keycloak or creating ARIA's client and roles — the Identity epic owns those; this story consumes the issuer URL, client id and secret. Standing up Ollama is also out, one already runs on the GPU node — but per D28 its server configuration is in scope.

**Acceptance criteria**

* A clean apply creates the namespace and one ServiceAccount per deployed service (`aria-gateway`, `aria-speech`, `aria-agent-core`, `aria-mcp-registry`, `aria-knowledge-core`); re-applying is a no-op
* `aria-identity` is explicitly absent from the deployed set — it is a library crate, not a workload
* A default for resource requests/limits is documented and demonstrated on a sample workload, sized for one person plus a small circle
* A throwaway pod reaches the existing Keycloak issuer and Ollama endpoint recorded by ARIA-79, and creates no new instance of either
* Both endpoints reach workloads as configuration, so changing one needs a restart, not an image rebuild
* A placeholder secret reaches a pod as an env var or mounted file via a SealedSecret committed to git and decrypted in-cluster; no plaintext is committed
* Namespace resources are delivered by the umbrella `aria` chart — one release, one `values.yaml` — not per-service charts or ad-hoc manifests
* Each service's Keycloak confidential-client credentials carry the per-callee audience scopes encoding which services it may call
* Ollama's ARIA-managed server configuration (residency, concurrency, model preloading) is recorded as chart-managed state, not undocumented drift

**Decisions**

* D5 — the credentials delivered here are confidential-client credentials whose scopes encode the call graph
* D13 — CI runs on GitHub-hosted runners; sealing needs only the cluster's **public** certificate, so no private key leaves the network
* D15 — one umbrella Helm chart for the namespace
* D28 — ARIA may reconfigure the shared Ollama, so its server settings belong in the chart
* D31 — sealed-secrets; the controller is ARIA-112, its private key is backup state under ARIA-96
* D34 — the same mechanism carries credentials for newly approved self-generated services

issues.description:
A `tonic` interceptor in `aria-mcp-registry` that extracts and verifies the Gateway's signed context using the shared `aria-identity` crate, and makes the resolved caller the only identity available to the rest of the service. Both consent gates and the audit log depend on the Registry having the _right_ `user_id`, so this lands before either gate is built.

**Acceptance criteria**

* Any `ListTools` or `CallTool` arriving without a valid signed user context is rejected `UNAUTHENTICATED` before any MCP server is contacted and before any consent lookup happens
* A context that fails signature verification, or is expired/replayed under the Gateway's scheme, is rejected — covered by a test that mutates the `user_id` in an otherwise valid context
* The resolved caller is the single identity used by both consent gates and the audit log; a static check or test asserts no code path reads an identity out of a request body or tool-argument payload
* A `CallTool` whose arguments contain an identity-shaped field does not change the resolved caller — a test sends a spoofed `user_id` argument and asserts consent is evaluated against the metadata identity
* Authentication rejections are traced and counted separately from consent denials, so "who are you?" and "you may not do that" stay distinguishable in the Observability stack
* The reserved `_aria_user_id` argument is stripped from every tool schema the Registry exposes — a test asserts a tool that declares `_aria_user_id` still has it absent from the schema returned by `ListTools`
* The Registry sets `_aria_user_id` on every forwarded call from the resolved metadata identity, overwriting any incoming value unconditionally — a test pre-fills it with another user's id and asserts the forwarded call carries the metadata identity instead

**Decisions**

* D9 — enforcement identity and contextual identity are separated. Enforcement identity comes **only** from the Gateway's signed context metadata; contextual identity is a reserved `_aria_user_id` argument that the **Registry**, not the Agent Core, injects — stripped from model-visible schemas and overwritten unconditionally

**Links:** [Decision Log — identity & tokens](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/decisions/0001-identity-tokens-service-auth.md) · [MCP Registry](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/services/mcp-registry.md) · [Identity](https://github.com/FPGSchiba/aria/blob/main/docs/services/identity.md)

issues.description:
Define the correlation between two record-keeping systems that must not be confused — the
`consent_audit_log` (a security audit trail) and OpenTelemetry traces (operational telemetry with a  
hard content constraint) — and ship the API that makes it possible. One-way by design: the audit  
record references the trace, the trace never carries audit content.

**Not this story:** the `consent_audit_log` schema, its writes or its enforcement — owned by  
Knowledge Core and MCP Registry, and not to be duplicated here.

**Acceptance criteria**

* The observability crate exposes a small, documented API returning the current trace ID and span ID as opaque values, callable by any service without pulling in tracing internals
* The convention specifies that audit records carry the trace ID and span ID of the operation that produced them, as correlation fields — an audit row points at a trace
* The convention specifies, and the attribute allow-list enforces, that a span may record that a consent decision occurred and its outcome as a bounded value, and must **not** record the prompt text, the tool arguments, or the data the decision governed
* An integration test writes an audit record during a traced operation and asserts the recorded trace ID resolves to a real exported trace containing that operation — the correlation is usable, not merely present in a schema
* With audit-generating traffic driven through the system, no consent prompt text or tool argument appears in any exported span
* The ownership boundary is written into the story's outcome documentation: the table belongs to Knowledge Core, its writes and enforcement to MCP Registry, and this epic owns only the trace-ID API and the correlation convention

**Open**

* Retention divergence: an audit trail typically outlives operational telemetry by a wide margin, so a trace ID in an audit row will often resolve to a trace that no longer exists. Whether that is acceptable, or whether the audit row should snapshot a minimal trace summary, is not decided — and telemetry retention is itself undecided

issues.description:
The Registry-side writer. "Allowed **or denied**" is the load-bearing part: a denial that leaves no trace is as bad as an unlogged success. Built before the two consent gates, because each gate's denial path must land in this log.

**Not this story:** the `consent_audit_log` table and its schema belong to the Knowledge Core epic; this story appends through the Knowledge Core's API.

**Acceptance criteria**

* An entry is appended for every `CallTool` attempt reaching the Registry — including calls denied by either gate and calls that fail because the target server errored or was unreachable; entry count equals attempt count for a scripted mixed sequence
* Each entry records at minimum caller `user_id`, server id, tool name, decision (allowed / denied), the denial reason where applicable, and a timestamp; the `user_id` is the one from the Gateway's signed context, never one taken from tool arguments
* Denial reasons stay distinguishable — server-level consent missing or revoked, per-tool grant missing, unknown tool, and downstream failure are not collapsed into one generic "denied"
* Tool arguments and results are not written wholesale; whatever payload detail is recorded is bounded, documented in the ticket, and covered by a test asserting a large argument payload does not reach the entry
* A failed audit write for a _denied_ call never causes the call to be allowed — the denial stands and the write failure is surfaced as an error signal
* Consent prompts are auditable in their own right: a `consent required` outcome, the user's grant-or-refuse answer and the automatic retry are each distinct entries, so a scripted prompt-grant-retry sequence yields a record from which the grant's origin is reconstructable

**Decisions**

* D42 — conversational granting means a grant can come into existence mid-conversation, so prompts and their outcomes are audit events too, not only invocations

**Open**

* Whether a failed audit write for an _allowed_ call fails the call closed (strict auditability) or is retried / queued for later write

**Not this story:** CI for build, test, lint and protobuf codegen — Platform Foundation epic. Application code inside each image — each service's own epic.

comments.body:
**Decided 2026-08-19 (D51): the container registry is GitHub Container Registry (**`ghcr.io`).

No registry is stood up in the homelab.

**Why.** D13 already put CI on GitHub Actions, and `ghcr.io` is the registry that comes with it — a workflow can push using the automatically-provided `GITHUB_TOKEN`, with no additional credential to provision, rotate or seal. An in-cluster registry would be another stateful workload to run, secure and back up, standing between "no code" and "first image" — and the cluster is now known to be **two nodes** (see ARIA-79) with no shared storage established, so registry storage would itself need solving first.

It also composes cleanly with **D45**, which makes an MCP server's identity its **image digest**: `ghcr.io` returns digests on push, so the approval artifact can record exactly what CI produced. This story's existing criterion about recording digests rather than only tags is therefore straightforwardly satisfiable.

**Rejected.** _An in-cluster registry_ (`registry:2` or Harbor) — keeps images on the LAN and removes an external dependency from the deploy path, but it is a stateful workload with its own storage, TLS and backup story; Harbor additionally brings replication and scanning a one-person circle does not need. _Docker Hub_ — ubiquitous, but pull rate limits and public-by-default visibility are both wrong here.

**Consequence, recorded because it is not free.** D13 accepted that _"source and build logs leave the network"_, narrowing local-by-default to _"no **personal** data leaves"_. This extends it: **built artifacts now live off-site too.** The posture is unchanged in substance — images derive from source that already left — but CLAUDE.md §4's list of what crosses the network boundary gains a fourth entry and should say so, rather than let a reader infer that images stay home.

**Direct follow-through for this story and ARIA-91.** Private `ghcr.io` packages require an `imagePullSecret` on the pulling nodes. Under **D31** that is a sealed secret like any other. Making the packages public would avoid the secret entirely, at the cost of publishing what ARIA is built from — worth deciding deliberately rather than by default. Whether the nodes already carry an `imagePullSecret` for anything else is being checked by the ARIA-79 baseline run.

Full reasoning: `docs/decisions/0009-measurement-session.md`, entry D51.

issues.description:
The outer of the two consent layers, checked at call time: for this user and this server, does Keycloak-level consent still stand.

**Not this story:** provisioning the per-MCP-server client, its declared scopes, the consent screen and the account-console revocation UX belong to the Keycloak epic (ARIA-38). This story owns only the check.

**Acceptance criteria**

* Before any call is forwarded, the Registry resolves the target server's Keycloak client and checks the caller's consent for it against Keycloak — not against a local flag the Registry itself can set
* A user who revoked consent in the account console has their next `CallTool` for that server denied with `PERMISSION_DENIED` and the server is never contacted; verified end-to-end against the real homelab Keycloak, not a stub
* A user who has never consented to that server is denied the same way, with a reason distinct from "revoked"
* Both denials reach `consent_audit_log` marked as a server-level consent failure, distinguishable from a per-tool grant failure
* Consent lookups may be cached only with a bounded TTL or an explicit invalidation path; a test proves a revocation takes effect within that bound, and the bound is documented in the ticket
* The gate fails closed: Keycloak unreachable or erroring denies and audits rather than allows
* The TTL is \~30 s and an entry that expires and cannot be refreshed denies: one test proves revocation lands within 30 seconds, a second proves a Keycloak outage during refresh denies rather than permitting on a stale entry

**Decisions**

* D43 — the acceptable staleness bound is a \~30 s TTL on the cached Keycloak-level consent read, and an entry that cannot be refreshed fails closed

**Open**

* Which exact Keycloak mechanism reads a user's granted consents at call time — admin REST grant lookup, token exchange, or introspection of a per-server token. D43 fixes the caching and failure behaviour, not the API underneath; the investigation is **owned by this story**, to be agreed with the Keycloak Integration epic
